The Karnataka State Transport Corporation, the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation and some other private operators filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the vires of section 63(7) of the . The High Court set aside the grant of three out of eleven permits to the Karnataka state Tourism Development Corporation and increased the number of permits granted to the Indian Tourism Development Corpora tion from one to three. The Tribunal took the view that having regard to the rule of preference enunciated by the proviso to section 63 (7), the applications from the 'non preferred ' category had to be excluded as the number Of applications from applicants who were required to be given preference exceeded the number specified in the proviso, and that the grant was set aside. The High court also took the same view. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of some of the private operators that the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Court were wrong in distinguishing the decision of this Court in Sher Singh 's case and that in the case of the court interpreted the word 'preference ' occurring in section 47(1 H) in the back ground of the provisions of Chapters IV and IV A of the Act, under the former of which the State transport Undertaking would have preference whereas under the latter the State Road transport Corporation would have a monopoly. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The general scheme of the Motor Vehicles Act in the matter of grant of permits for stage carriages and contract carriages appears to be that except in the cases of a notified route or notified area where under section 68 F(1) the permit has to be necessarily granted to tho State Transport Undertaking, in all other cases, the claims of all eligible applicants must be considered on merits, applying the rules of preference wherever the claims are approximately equal. The proviso to Section 47(I H) for example, provides that in case of inter State route, the Undertaking will have preference in the matters of stage carriage permit. [1015C D] 2. Clause (iv) of section 47 (1 H), for example provides that other conditions being equal, an application for a stage carriage permits from a cooperative society or a person holding a valid licence for driving transport vehicles shall as far as may be, be given priority over applications from individual owners. [ 1015E] 3. The word 'repreference" in section 2(25) is unconstitutional and it is not necessary that the department is able to exercise some control on the functioning of these operators. [10F] 4. Clause(iv) provides for a preference, not to operators of tourist vehicles but to operators or of tourist cars and travel agents. Though the permits to be granted are for tourist vehicles, the preference is confined to operators who of tourist car and travel agent. Although the permits are for Tourist vehicles, it mentions that approval carries with it certain privileges, such as allotment of ex STC vehicles and that it is, therefore, necessary that they should be owning and operating five vehicles as tourist taxies of either indigenous make or acquired from elsewhere regardless of the period in the car hire business or that they must be ex Defence Service personnel, who satisfy certain prescribed conditions. The matter appears to have been left to the total discretion of the Central Government, virtually as we said, pre empting the decision. [1005C E] Sher Singh vs Union of India, ; , referred to.

The respondent purchased, by a registered instrument dated October 5, 1956, the business carried on by one Purushottam Raju under the name All India Trading Company. Purushottam Raju was the sole proprietor of the business and had been assessed to sales tax in respect of his turnover for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The assessee paid some amounts towards sales tax thus determined but there remained some arrears of sales tax i.e., Rs. 3836 4 0 for 1948 49, and Rs. 1218 1 9 for 1949 50 The Sales Tax authorities attempted to recover the arrears of tax from the respondent as the purchaser of the said business. The respondent 6 63 denied liability to pay sales tax but his contention was over ruled by the Deputy Commercial Tax Officer. The appellant then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the orders of the Commercial Tax officer and the Board of Revenue. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that Rule 21 A was ultra vires of the rule making power of the State Government under section 19(1) and (2) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The word 'assessment ' used in section 19 (2)(c) does not include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other than the assessee. It follows therefore that Rule is beyond the rulemaking power of State Government either under section19(1), or section 19, (2). [665 B] Badridas Daga vs C.I.T., Bihar, ; Chatturam vs C I.T. Bihar, , Chattaram vs C., I. T. Bihar and Chattamuram vs Commissioner of Inland Revenue, A. 1. R. , referred to.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the Inspector General of Prisons, Saurashtra. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the order of dismissal was illegal and void on the ground that it contravened article 311(2) of the Constitution. The trial court held that the failure on the part of the competent authority to provide the appellant with a copy of the report of the Enquiry Officer amounted to denial of reasonable opportunity contemplated by article 311 (2). On appeal, the District Judge confirmed the order and dismissed the suit. In second appeal, he contended that the High Court erred in holding that there had been a breach of article 311 as according to him there was no duty to supply a copy thereof. Held, that the appellant was entitled under the Workmen 's Compensation Act, 1906 to compensation from the shipowners not only in respect of his wages but also of the retainer, which must be taken into account as earnings under a concurrent contract of service. The liability to pay salary when it has been fixed arises out of a contract to pay wages. In the present case, the liability to payment of arrears of pay was not a liability arising out of any contract but was a liability in respect Of an actionable wrong other than breach of contract. The decree of the High court decreeing payment of wages was truly a liability and it could not be said that the Government servant was not prejudiced by the non supply of the copy of report of Enquiry Officer. State of Bihar vs Abdul Majid, ; , referred to. Held further, that in the present ease, the appellant had failed to prove that he had been given reasonable opportunity within the meaning of article 313(2). The High Court was right in holding, that there was a breach on his part and that the refusal by the competent officer to provide him with a copies of the reports of the enquiry held against him amounted to violation of article 14.

The appellant was granted a lease of the coal and coal mining rights in respect of 400 bighas out of his total area. The lease deed provided that the northern boundary of the leasehold land was to be drawn between the two leaseholds. The western boundary was shown as the northern boundaries of the lease hold of Samanta. On June 15,1900, the appellant made an inquiry and came to know that the defendants had encroached upon their coal mines on the northern side and removed coal from the encroached portion and had rendered the remaining coal of the encroached portions unworkable. The Commissioner appointed by the Court tested the position of the six trijunction pillars shown in the map of lease dated November 23, 1900, and found that two of the trijram pillars were in their correct positions. On these allegations the appellant asked for the following reliefs: (a) That the intermediate boundary line between the appellants ' coal land and the defendants ' coal mining right be ascertained and fixed; (b)That a permanent injunction be issued against the defendants restraining them from encroaching upon the plaintiffs ' coal mines and removing coal therefrom. The respondents denied that they had encroached on the plaintiff ' coal lands and stated that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court held that the defendant had encroached Upon the appellant 's coal land, that the lease deed was not a valid document and that the boundary could more satisfactorily be fixed with reference to the plans annexed to the subsequent lease deeds executed in favour of the successors in interest of the appellant and the respondents. On appeal the High Court accepted all the findings of the trial court and dismissed the appeal. Held: (i) The finding of the courts below that the disputed extent of land was part of the holding of the respondents, is vitiated by an error of law by the burden of proof having been wrongly thrown on the appellant. (ii) The onus was upon the plaintiff in these suits to prove that the knowledge of his father wag within three years of the suit and that is all. If he proves this, then to succeed in the plea of limitation the defendant has to prove satisfactorily that the fact that the property was in his possession became known to the plaintiff more than three years prior to the suit. (iii) The burden of proving that the title was in the possession of the defendant within three year of the date of filing of the suits, and that was all. , therefore, on the respondents it could not be held that they were guilty of any breach of contract.

The appellant, a saw mill in the State of Kerala, was in the employ of the appellant as a crosscutter. It was alleged that on June 21, 1958, Sankaran came drunk to them mill and abused them with physical violence. He was caught hold of by other workmen and taken outside. The appellant served a charge sheet on Sankaran on June 24, 1958 acting out the above facts and asked him to show cause why his services should not be terminated on account of his grave indiscipline and misconduct. Sankaran gave an explanation the same day denying the allegations of fact made against him though he admitted that he had come to the mill at the relevant time for taking his wages for that week. On July 8, 1958 Sankaran again wrote to the appellant to hold the inquiry as early as possible. On August 9, 1958 the appellant terminated the services of Sankaran under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders without holding any departmental enquiry and the order was communicated to Sankaran. The Industrial Tribunal held that something seemed to have happened on the afternoon of June 21. 1958 but there was no evidence to prove what had actually happened. It further held that the appellant had intended to take disciplinary action against the workman but subsequently departmental proceedings were dropped and action was taken under r, 18(b) of Standing Orders. The Tribunal also pointed out that no attempt was made before it to defend the action taken under rule 18 (a) by proving the alleged misconduct. Two witnesses were produced before the tribunal in connection with the alleged offence but the Tribunal did not rely on them on the ground that the important witnesses, namely, the Engineer, the Secretary and other members of the staff whose evidence would have been of more value had not been produced and no explanation had been given why they were not produced. The tribunal therefore held that on the facts it could not come to its conclusion that Sankaran had come drunk to the Mill and abused or attempted to assault either the Engineer or the Secretary or the other officers. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The Industrial Court has the right to inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of service even under a rule like 18(A). The employer could defend the actions under r . 18(c) by leading evidence before the Tribunal to show that there was in fact misconduct and therefore the action was bona fide and was not colourable exercise of the power under that rule. (ii) Even if the inquiry was not held by the appellant and action taken thereunder, it is now well settled that the employer could dismiss the action under r ' 18(d).

The appellants were the owners of a theatre. The receivers granted a lease of the theatre on certain terms and conditions to two persons, Raval and Faraqui. By an agreement dated November 27, 1954, between Raval and Garaquii on the one hand and Messrs. Filmistan Distributors (India) Private Ltd., hereinafter called "Filmistan" instituted suit No. 149 of 1960 in the Court of Small Causes Ahmedabad against Raval and two other persons claiming a declaration that it was entitled pursuant to the agreement dated December 1, 1960, to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. By order dated December 31, 1960 the suit was disposed of as compromised. It was inter alia agreed that Raval and Earaqua were bound and liable to allow Filmistans to exercise their "exhibition rights" in the Theatre; that Raval, their servants and agents were not to have any right to exhibit any picture in contravention of the terms and condi tions of the agreement. The trial Judge passed an order disallowing the objection raised by the appellants. The revision application against that order was dismissed in limine by the High Court. When the case reached hearing and the evidence of a representative of Filmistna was being recorded, counsel for the defendants asked in cross examination the question whether the "agreement between the plaintiff and the defendant Nos. 5 and 6 were barred on principles of res judicata" from agitating the question that the said document dated November 1, 1954 as confirmed by their letter dated January 31, 1955 and further confirmed by document dated December l, 1960 was not a lease; and that in any event the suit No 149 of 1961 was for declaration of the rights of Films to exhibit cinematograph films, in view of section 92 of the Evidence Act. The High Court dismissed the revision application. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants (i) that an enquiry into the nature of the legal relationship arising out of the document could be permitted to 'be put to the witnesses for Filmisthan; and (ii) that the consent decree in suit No, 149 of 1953 had not decided that the agreement was of the nature Of a lease. HELD : (i). The order passed by the trial court is set aside and the Trial Court is directed to proceed and dispose of the suit. [446 E] (ii). A consent decree accord ing to the decisions of this Court, does not operate as res judicata, because a consent decree is merely the record of a contract between the parties to a suit, to which is superadded the seal of the court. A matter in contest in a suit may operate as Res judicata only if there is an adjudication by the Court : the terms of section II of the Code leave no scope for a contrary view. [441 G] (iii) The expression "case" is not limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action. This Court observed in Major section Khanna vs Brig. F. J. Dillon, [1893] 1 K.B.D. 426, that the expression " case" is a word of comprehensive import and includes a civil proceeding and is not restricted by anything contained in section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code to the extent to which the Court, viz., the trial Court in the instant case, proposed to go into that question and allow the whole question, that was closed once for all by consent decree of December 1.

The respondent, a pilot Officer was granted a permanent commission in the Indian Air Force and was, therefore, inval idated from I.A.F. The Government of India issued a scheme for the benefit of ex military officials. The State of Uttar Pradesh also adopted the same scheme. Under that scheme the ex military official were appointed on contract basis for a fixed term which could be extended from time to time subject to the suitability of the official concerned but not beyond 58 years of age. Pursuant to the said scheme the respondent was appointed as Secretary in the District Soldiers Board in the district of Unnao in the State of U.P. The terms and conditions contained in the said order included the above term relating to the period of appointment and on his accepting the terms and condi tion he was appointed to the post till 30th August, 1985 and it was again extended upto 31st March, 1983 by an order dated 1st June, 1983. Again the term was extended upto 30th of August,1985 by an Order dated 1 6 1983. The respondent was required to furnish his acceptance of the terms & conditions contained therein includ ing the above terms relating to period of appoint ment and on accepting the term and conditions he was appoint ed as Secretary. The order was to be effective from the date of receipt of termination order and no charges were men tioned therein against the 1st respondent. The Respondent aggrieved by the said orders filed a Writ Petition before the High Court contending that he was entitled to salary upto the period he was enti tled to remain in service, i.e., 30th September, 1985 unless there was a further extension. But on 29.3.1985 the service of the 1 st respondent was terminated by the issue of a notice and payment of one month 's salary. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition holding that the termination order could not be sustained and the Writ petition was liable to be allowed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the interim order entitled him to be reinstated in service irrespective of the fact whether the Governor had extended the period beyond 30th 885 of August 1985. Allowing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court has while setting aside the order of termination by its order dated 24.3 1988 directed that the respondent be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to con tinue till he completed the age of 58 years. Even the order passed on Review on 26.7.1988 does not make out that the Respondent had put forward at that stage such a case.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not sufficient to convict him as they were interested in the incident and that the discrepancies noticed by the Sessions Judge were of a minor character and that they had been unduly magnified by the learned Sessions Judge. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High court was justified in interfering with the order of acquittal merely because another view is also possible. [368E] (2) It is well settled that at one time it was thou nt that an order of conviction could be set aside for "substantial and compelling reasons" only and Courts used to launch on a search to discover those "substantial & compelling reasons". However, the circumstances were possible on the evidence and the accused was entitled to the benefit of doubt arising from the two views and that where the Trial Court has taken a possible view and acquitted the accused, the High Court should not interfere with the acquittal merely on the ground that another view was also possible.[368F H] Sanwat Singh & Ors. vs State of Rajasthan, ; , followed. (3) The discrepancies were in regard to which of them woke up first, where was the lantern and which of the neighbours came first to the scene on hearing their cries. The witnesses were of such a nature that they could have been seen by the persistent refusal of the brother and mother of the deceased to send her with him to his house. He probably attributed the refusal to reluctance on the part of his wife to accompany him straightaway. [369A B] Sanwar Singh & ors. vs The State of Bihar, ; and Sanwat Sing & Ors., vs State, A.l. R. , referred to. (4) In the instant case, the evidence was corroborated by the evidence given by the prosecution witnesses. It is true that the accused did not have any deep motive to kill the deceased. It was obvious that he must have been upset by the constant refusal of brother and her mother to send the deceased with him for a thumb impression on which the deceased was sleeping. The evidence of P. Ws. 4 and 5 who came to the spot soon afterwards, could not be said to have been caused in the manner suggested by the accused. [370E F] Sanat Singh & Anr.

The appellant was a Judge of the Supreme Court. He was convicted for having committed an offence under section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court dismissed his appeal and convicted him. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that (i) the President is given the power to appoint the Judges of the High Court as well as of the Chief Justice of the high Court by warrant under his hand and seal after consultation with the Chief justice of India, the Governor of the State and in a case of appointment of a Judge other than the Chief Jus tice, the Chief Judge of a High Court can be removed from his office by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a minority of not less then two thirds of the members of that house present and voting, has been presented to the President in the same session for such removal on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity; (ii) the power under clause (c) is the President and it is in this manner that section 6(1) (c), which specifically enjoins that no court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 161(or section 165 of the Indian Penal Code, or under sub section (2) or sub section 3A) of section 5 of this Act, alleged to have been committed by a public servant, except with the previous sanction, (a) in the case of any other person, of the authority competent to remove him from his Office; and (b) in case of a person who is employed in connection with the affairs of the Union and is not removable from his offices save by or with the sanction of the Central Government. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power to punish a High court Judge, if one may so describe it, is to be found only in article 2 read with Article 124(4) and (5) of Article 124 of the Constitution. [835C] 2.1 In the case, the President has not been given the sole power or the exclusive power to remove a Judge either of the, Supreme Court or of theHigh Court from his place in order to enable that authority to grant sanction for prosecution of the Judge under the provisions of section 6 of the Act and this can be done only if it is read as a part of the scheme under which the public servant is required to furnish particulars of his assets with reference to which such an opinion can be formed and there is no vertical superior with legal authority enabling obtaining of information from the concerned Judge. [889E] 2:2 The President, therefore, being the authority Competent to appoint and to remove Judge, of course in accordance with the procedure envisaged in Article 124, clauses (4) & (5), placed before the President, a Judge by warrant, under his hands and seal, after consultationwith such of the Judges. [879E F] 2 :3 The power of appointment and removal of a judge other than those of the highest Court is not contemplated by section 6, but only for the purpose of deciding whether the offence under clause(e) of possession of disproportionate assets which the Public servant cannot satisfactorily account is made out prima facie. [869C] 4:1. The President has no power or authority to remove any Judge either from his residence or from his post except with a previous sanction.

The appellant was a member of a Scheduled Caste. Abhoy Pada Saha and Sudhir Kumar Mondal were the former was declared elected. The respondent challenged the validity of the order of the High Court rejecting his prayer to be declared elected, on various grounds. At the hearing of the petition by the Election Tribunal, however, he challenged the election only on the ground that Abhiman Pada was a Member of the Saha caste and not a member thereof. The Election Tribunal rejected this contention and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The appellant was not a Sunri by caste and had not been proved to belong to the smaller caste group of Sahas. He must be held to belong lo the Scheduled Caste specified in item 40. [390 E] (ii) The Tribunal was wrong in considering the Sahas as an independent caste. [391 C] (iii) The expression "excluding" denoted that the Saha ' contemplated would, but for this word had come within the Sunri caste. It is legitimate to think that when a statute says that a thing is to be excluded from another, both things are of the same kind; if one is a caste. the other must be a caste; it follows that when the item excluded Sahas from Sunris, since Sunri was a caste group, Saha must equally be another caste group. [392 E G] (iv) The finding that Sahas were a 'a group within the ' Sunri Caste ' is irrelevant as a test for applying item 40 unless it is shown that it indicated a smaller caste Group of Sunris. It was not necessary that such part must necessarily form a sub caste. The Tribunal, therefore, rightly held that the appellant had failed to prove that the respondent belonged to a smaller community group of ' Sahas and was thereby excluded from the Scheduled Castes specified in Item 40 for he said "these Saha families, within the fold of Sunri castes".

The appellant was the tenant of a flat on the second floor of a building called "Ganga Vihar", Marine Drive, Bombay. The tenancy was a monthly one, the rent being Rs. 215. It is said that the appellant wanted to go to the United Kingdom for treatment of his failing eye sight and he got into touch with the police on 1 12 1948, and in conjunction with the latter, a trap was laid for the appellant. The complainant and the Sub Inspec tor were then taken to the appellant 's residence on 4 12 1948 and in connection with the raid held up the car of the appellant and recovered the sum of Rs. 30,500 from the rear seat of the car and also some papers, a typed draft of a partnership agreement was tween the complainant and his wife and the appellant, an application form for permission to occupy the building as caretaker. The appellant was charged under section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, for receiving a pugree of Rs 29,500 and he was further charged under s 19(2) of that Act for receiving the said sum as a condition for the relin quishment of his tenancy. The defence of the appel lant was that he was in search of a partner to carry on his business during his intended absence, who was also to act as caRetaker of his flat anal that it was in this connection and with this object in view of his intended departure. The prosecution case was that the accused demanded a sum of RS. 30 lakhs which was later on reduced to Rs. 29, 500 as consideration for putting the complainant in vacant possession of the flat and an additional amount of Rs 2,000 for the furniture, and that the complainant agreed to pay these sums. The wife of the deceased denied any aiding and abetting. The Presidency Magistrate who tried the case convicted him under section 19(1)(c) of 'the Act and sentenced him to one month 's simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs 30,000. The appeal preferred by the appellant was summarily dismissed on 20 2 1950. On 10 4 1950 the wife of appel late was acquitted, the evidence being insufficient to prove any abetment. The High Court rejected this contention on behalf of the appellants based on the language of section 19 (1) and this is the only point which required our consideration. Held:(i) An assignment of the lease or transfer in any other manner by a tenant is not made an offence; the statute merely says that it is not a lawful transaction. It was the landlord 's consent to the transfer of a lease by sub lease or otherwise on receipt of consideration that has been made an offen cientence. The section in question, it should be further noted does not speak of relinquishment or giving up of possession,in general terms. (ii) In the case of an assignment, the assignor contin ues to be liable to the landlord for the performance of his obligations under the tenancy and this liability is contrac tual, while the assignee becomes liable by reason of privity of estate. The consent of the landlord to an assignment is not necessary in the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary. But in the case Of relinquishment, it cannot be a unilateral transaction; it can only be in favour of the lessor by mutual agreement between them. (iii) In fact, a surrender or relinquishment terminates the lessee 's rights and lets in the lessor. It could only be made in favour o the lessor through mutual agreement. The relin cation of possession must be to the lessor or one who holds his interest.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was a partnership and the workmen of the Tata Engineering Company were members of the Hindustan Shipyard Limited. The company functions as a consulting organisation and a service industry, and does not manufacture any product or carry on trade. Its work force consists of engineers and supervisors and different categories of workmen. Out of these employees at Bombay, the draftsmen and the administrative staff number 306. These workmen are members of Tata Engineering Co. Ltd., and they served a Charter of Demands in July 1974 on the appellant and as their demands were not accepted and conciliation proceedings proved fruitless, the State Government made a reference of the dispute under section 10(1) (d), Industrial Tribunal, Maharashtra for adjudication. The Reference was numbered I. T. No. 292 of 1975. The claim of the Union was resisted by the appellant who maintained that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the union were accepted. But it rejected the demand of the company for dearness allowance on the basis of slab system, because that would have imposed an unacceptable burden on the Appellant 's financial capacity and there was no reason why the existing scheme of dearness allowance should be disturbed when a substantial increase was being made in the level of the basic wage. The Tribunal also noted that after the salaries of the employees had been fixed in the respective scales, senior employees would have to be given some more increments in the new scales according to their completed years of service. Rs. 150/ and Rs. 100/ were added to the pay of every other workman, who belonged to the Union staff, the financial load would increase to Rs.100/ was given to individual workmen of all categories including Draughtsmen, the increased financial load will total Rs. 50/ and above the existing pay scales. The appellant 's application before the Tribunal was contested by the Union contending that the amendment results in the inclusion of a flat increase of Rs.150/ to each workman in the case of Draughtsman and Rs., 100/ and that there was nothing in the body of the award to form the foundation on which the actual figures in the restructured pay scales could be made to rest. The Industrial Tribunal rejected the contention of the appellant that a flat increased to the Pay of each workman was intended in the original wage and, consequently, it fell into the error of amending the award. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the workmen. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the corrigendum was in effect a fresh award and, therefore, falling beyond the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. On behalf of respondent Union it was submitted that the appellant was bound by the order made on the application. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The terms of reference in the State government 's order required the Tribunal to revise the scales of pay and dearness allowance, and there is no mention of giving any ad hoc increase in the basic pay of individual workman. The financial capacity, as the Tribunal observed, constituted one of "the principles which are required to be followed in the fixation of the wage structure". A clear statement of its intention is found in paragraph 22 of the Award where the Tribunal stated: "I only propose to modify the existing structures of the scales with flat increases in each category." [177A B] 2. The award was a composite document in which the several elements of increased wage scales, larger increments, longer span of 20 years for earning increments, dearness allowance at 10% of the Basic wage, besides several other benefits, have been integrated into a balanced arrangement in keeping with what the Tribunal has found to be the financial capacity of the Appellant.

The appellant, Sasamusa Sugar Works Ltd., and its workmen, the respondents an award had been made by an Industrial Tribunal fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/2/ per day, and in pursuance thereof, the management of the appellant had entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the said award. This agreement was subsequently published in Bihar Gazette as a part of the award. In spite of the Award and the agreement, the appellant paid its employees only As. / 10/ per month and that led to the present claim made by the respondents under section 15 of the Act. The respondents contended before the payment of wages authority that the refusal of the appel lant to pay to them wages at the rate awarded in substance amounted to an illegal deduction from their wages, and on that basis they asked for an order from the authority directing the appellant to pay the said prescribed wages. The appellant raised two pleas against the respondents ' claim. It was urged that section 15 Of the Act was inapplicable because the rates of wages fixed by the award did not fall within the definition of wages prescribed by section 2(vi) and it also argued, that the claim of the respondents was barred by limitation. The authority rejected the appellant 's contention and held that section 2 (vi) included wages prescribed under the Industrial Tribunal Act, and so it had rejected the appellants ' contention that the applications made by them were incompetent under section15 of the , and dismissed the petition. Held: (i) The basic assumption made by Mr. Setalvad in contending that section2(vi)(a) cannot take in the wages prescribed in the award is not well founded. When an award is made and it prescribes a new wage structure, in law the old contractual wage structure becomes inoperative and its place is taken by the wage structures prescribed by it. In a sense, the latter wage structure must be deemed to be a contract between the parties, because that, in substance, is the effect of industrial adjudication. The true legal position is that when industrial disputes are decided by industrial adjudication and awards are made, the said awards supplant contractual terms in respect of matters covered by them and are substituted for them. That being so, it is difficult to accede to the argument that the wages fixed under the award cannot be treated as wages under section 2.(vi) of the Industrial Disputes Act before it was amended. (ii) The amendment has merely clarified what, in our opinion, was included in the unamended definition itself. In this connection, the South Indian Bank Ltd. vs A. R. Chacko, A.I.R. 1964 S.C. 1523, and V. B Godse, Manager, Prabha Mills Ltd., vs R. M. Naick Inspector, under the Payment of Wages Act, the Bombay High Court has interpreted section 2 of the . (iii) to include wages directed to be paid by industrial adjudica tion.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department of Pepsu. He was charged with having dishonestly removed certain medicines from a hospital which he had taken to his residence and misappropriated them. The trial court convicted him under section 465, Indian Penal Code for forging the thumb impression of Parma, and under section 409 of the Indian Penal code for criminal misappropriation of Rs. 51 shown as paid to him for his wages. On appeal by the State Government the High Court held that proof that the thumb impressions in the acquittance roll were that of the appellant was sufficient to establish an offence either under section 466 or section 409, and that there having been an acquittal of the accused by the trial Magistrate, the materials on record did not justify a reversal of that verdict by the appellate court. The State appealed to this Court with certificate granted by the High Courts. It was contended for the appellant that the prosecution had failed to establish that the amount drawn by him did not reach the hands of Parama and that therefore no sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure could be taken against him. Held, that the conviction of the respondent was illegal as sanction under s. 197(I) of Code of criminal procedure was necessary for prosecuting a public servant under section409 of the Government of India Act, 1935, and the absence of such sanc tion was fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. The fact that the appellant had been acquitted by the Trial Court did not affect his conviction. The sanction under S. 197 (1) was required only in cases where the official character of the person giving the information was found to be irrelevant or extraneous. The mere fact that a public officer was involved in the very act complained of as amounting to a crime, would not make him liable for prosecution under section 196(1). Hori Ram Singh vs Emperor, A.I.R. 1948 Pat. 75, approved.

The assessee was a public limited company incorporated in the State of Cochin with branches in that State as well as in what was British India and in Travancore State. It filed its income for the assessment year 1948 49, its accounting year being the previous calendar year. The Income tax Officer determined its assessable income to be Rs. 90 representing only the profit it made in Travancore state and under section 32(1) proviso (i) of the Travancore Act he refused a deduction of Rs. 79,275 shown as loss from branches situate outside the State. The assessee 's appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was unsuccessful but the Appellate Tribunal held that the banking business of the assessee being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax it was entitled to deduct the losses incurred outside Travancore State from the profits accruing and arising in that state. At the instance of the Commissioner of Income tax the following question was referred to the High Court of Travancore Cochin: " Whether on the facts and circumstances of the case the loss of Rs 27,709 arising in Cochin State could be set off against the profit of Rs." The assessee contended that the first proviso to section 24(1)(i) did not apply to the head business business but only introduced an addendum that where the profits of the business arose in what is British India in the case of Travancore Act and the losses under the head 'business were sustained in an Indian State or in the latter case in any other Indian State, these losses could not by virtue of the proviso be deducted from profits made in British India or Travancore State as the case may be. Held, that the object of section 24 was to allow a set off of profits arising under different heads and only in such cases could recourse be had to section 25(1). Arunachalam Chettiar vs Commissioner of Incometax, Madras ([1950] S.C.R. 271), Ram Narain Sons Ltd. vs Assistant Commissioner of Sales Tax (2) , distinguished.

The first respondent, Shaw Wallace & Co., was incorporated in January 1946 as a Private Limited Company to take over the business of the partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace and Co. The Head Office of the Company is at Calcutta. It has branches in Bombay, Delhi and Via Madras. The general practice of the company both at the Head Office and the Branch Offices appears to have been to retire its employees at the age of 55 though in certain cases the Company in its discretion permitted an employee to continue beyond that age. In September 1959 an agreement was entered into between the Company and its employees under which the age Of retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the ageof 55. The first respondent raised a dispute regarding their retirement age but the Tribunal directed that the age should be 58 but the Company may in its wisdom and with the express or implied consent of the employee concerned continue an employee after he attains that age, and it was also found that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Bombay region the trend had been to fix the retirement age at 60 years. The Tribunal further directed that in view of this finding of the Tribunal that in some of its earlier decisions as to the relevant trend in the Bombay region was accurate, the Tribunal took into account the fact that in the awards recent times there was a general agree ment that the date of retirement should be fixed at 60 and not at 55. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the decision of this Court in Dunzlop Rubber Co. Ltd., vs Workmen ; , relied on by the Tribunal was erroneous as the facts and circumstances disclosed by the oral and documentary evidence on record clearly showed a consistent trend in Bombay regions region to fix its retirement age. Held, further, that the Tribunal had taken considerable pains to perform this duty and it had ultimately persuaded itself to hold that no such trend was established in fact. Dunzoop Rubber Company Ltd., v The Workmen ; and Dunzyop Rubber CO. Ltd. vs Workmen, [1960] 2 S.C.R. 869, relied on.

The power conferred by section 239(b)(a) is merely administrative it is difficult to appreciate how the allocation of business of the Board relating to the exercise Of such power can be anything other than a matter of procedure. For sub section (6) of section 10 E, I am inclined to construe this rule making power liberally and the Central Govt has power to constitute the company 's board to control (1)(2) 342 The power is conferred on it but under the Companies Act, 1951, a Board of Company Law Administration consisting of a Chairman and a member has been set up.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 100/ . In appeal to this Court it was contended that the presumption that they were dacoits ought not to have been drawn since the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case, because dacoity as such is not challenged before this Court. HELD : The law advocated by Mr. Chari is not correct. If there is other evidence to connect an accused with the crime itself, however small the finding of the stolen property with him is a piece of evidence which connects him further with the offence. There is then no question of presumption. The evidence corroborating the other evidence already against him is sufficient to prove that he was concerned with the murder. [724 D E] In what circumstances the one presumption or the other may be drawn, it is not necessary to state categorically in this case. It all depends upon the circumstances under which the discovery of the fruits of crime are made with a particular accused. It has been stated on more than one occasion that if the gap of time is too large the presumption should be drawn. [624 D] In the present case, the goods stolen were not sold and were being taken back to the dealers by the cartmen. A large number of persons said to be 20 in number pelted stones at the cart men and looted the property. Immediately afterwards a number of searches were made and the goods were found with various persons who were prosecuted as offenders. The houses of 20 persons were searched and large quantities of the theft goods were recovered from them. It is impossible to think that within the short time available, these goods could have been easily disposed of to receivers of stolen property or could be placed in the custody of friends till such time as the original offenders could take them away.

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of "Tolinner" within the meaning of Section 5 of the , filed writ petitions in this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the vires of section 5 of Act XIII of 1919 (the Act) and for a direction to the State Government to include therein the substance as poison for purposes of restriction to be imposed on the possession of "unit is a manufacturing only those thinners which contain only liquid substance" like "discretions harmless in themselves". The petitioners contended that since the Act was a Central enactment it was possible of unjust and unjustified discrimination as it was left to each State Government, to determine what substance they would include as poison and regulated and the decision in one State to include the substance was unreasonable. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of neither Section 2 nor 5 nor the impugned notification are hit by any consti tutional limitation. [223E] 2. The Act is intended to regulate the importation, possession and sale of poisons. Some substances which the Government consider its possession for sale or sale to be regulated in the interest of health and safety of the society. This limitation is inherent in the scheme of the Act itself. Of course no comprehensive definition can be given to the word poison. Under this term it nobody can be considered to have an absolute right to carry on any trade or business. [222F] 3. The nature of trade in poison is such that nobody can he considered to be a poison for the entire country. The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance which would include "phenches of life". [223G] 4. Section 2(3) enables the Government by Rule to regulate possession, sale and sale in that area. It is a busi ness which can be termed even as inherently dangerous to health and fire safety of society in view of the rampant misuse and sale to the poor, weak and helpless as an intoxicant. A law in such circumstances can regulate the trade. This pos session is well settled and it would be pedantic to cite all the authorities of this Court on this point. [224H; 223A] 5. The Notification and its applica tion to any areas would depend upon the necessity for declaring the substance, as poison on the particular facts and situation prevailing in that locality and the need to regu lates the possession and sell ment of the same. No question of discrimination can arise in such circum stances. [225B] 6. The provision of neither section 2 nor5 nor the order are hit either by any provi sional limitation or is violative of any right to trade. [226C] 7. The writ petition accordingly fails and it is dismissed.

The appellants, who were the owners of a hotel in Calcutta, challenged the grant of four acres of land out of Begumbari Compound to India Hotel Co. The High Court held that the decision to lease the Begumbar land to the Taj Group of Hotels was taken on February 12, 1981 and that it was not forgotten that if the land was to be allotted to the Zoo logical Garden upon the terms set out in the two letters, there would still remain sufficient land for accommodating the existing facilities. The appellants filed an appeal before this Court against the decision of the High Court. On behalf of the appellants it was contended that the second Cabinet Memorandum dated September 9, 1981 on which date the Government took the final decision to grant the lease made no mention of the needs and interests of the Zooo or the facilities provided in the Begambari land for the Zoological Garden and there was no way by which the Government could divest the ZOogical Garden of the land except by a procedure known to law such as acquisition or requisition. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The proposed hotel is a Garden Hotel and there is perhaps every chance of the ecology and environment improving as a result of planting numerous trees all around the proposed hotel and the removal of the burial ground and burial ground for rubbish. [260F] 1.2 In the face of all these material facts, it cannot be seriously contended that there was an infinite variety of coniderations which may have to be taken into account by the Government in formulating its policies and it is on a total evaluation of various considerations which have weighed with the Govern ment in taking a particular action, that the Court would have to decide whether the action of the Government is reasonable and in public interest. [262G H] 1:3 The provisions of the Bengal Public Parks Act have no relevance to the question of the power of the government to transfer the Begumberland land to a Taj Group o f Hotels. The Chief Minister 's attention was expressly drawn to the Managing Committee 's first Resolution expressing its opposition to the proposal to give the land for construction of a Five Star Hotel on the Begangumbari land as a final decision, to the hotel group to start a Five star hotel, which according to the Government was a prime need to the city of Calcutta. The next question is whether the Government of West Bengal acted with probity in not inviting tenders or in not holding a public auction but negotiating straightaway at arm 's length with the Taj group of Hotels. [263A B] 1 :4 The provisions Of the BengalPublic Parks Act, 1904 have no relevancy to the ques tion of the powers of the Govern ing to transfer Begumbri land to an Taj Group. The Government was quite alive to the need for expan sion of the zoo when they decided to grant four acres Of Begumbli land which was not used for the main purpose of theZo for the construction of Five Star Hotels. It was also said that if, as the saying goes, the proof of the pudding is in the eating, the Chief Minister "s assurances are found reflected in the lease executed by the Taj Groups of Hotels in favour of the Govt. of WestBengal. The objection of the Public Undertakings Committee was first brought to the notice of the Minister for Metropolitan Development who submitted a note to the Chief Secretary pointing out that even if four acres were of land, out of the eight acres of Begambli land was given to the proposed hotels.

In the case of banking companies or other firms and companies who have overdraft facilities, even if the sums are not in credit of the donor and are not with such companies or firms, gifts might be possible by adjustment of the book entries. The circumstances must be such as to make it clear that there were sufficient funds at the disposal of the gifted donor by reason of which he could make the gift, by such book entries, and the firm in which he may have account may or may not have sufficient cash balance but it must have sufficient provision for overdraft with the bank on the basis it could honour in structions given by the assessee. The Orissa Superior Judicial Service (senior branch) is a combined cadre consisting of officers holding purely judicial posts as well as posts which are essentially administrative in character. It consists of eight district and sessions judges, two additional district and Sessions Judges, secretary to Government in law department, superintendent and legal remembrance and ex officio additional law secretary to the government in law Department, member administrative tribunal and the Registrar of the Orissa High Court, in all 15 in number. All these officers are the members of the service of the State and they were before 1962 presiding over district courts or courts subordinate to them and as such were under the control of the High Court. In view of article 229 of the Constitution, the power to appoint the Registrar is exclusively that of the Chief Justice. Neither the High Courts as such nor the Governor has any hand in his appointment. The power to transfer a district judge from one post to another whether as a Judge or to one of the posts in the secretariat was in his hands. It appears that for some time past there were differences between the High court and the Government about the posting of some judicial officers. The High Court was anxious that a judicial officer occupying one of these administrative posts enumerated above should not, in the interest of judicial work, continue in that post for an unduly long time. The Government by its letter of April 2, 1965 intimated that it had no objection to adhere to the principle of three years service in an appointment at a particular station against a special post. But when it came to the question of implementing that policy, the Government was reluctant. Every time the High ' Court requested the government to release the three officers mentioned above for being posted as district and Session judges or addl. district and session judges as the case may be, the government turned down those requests on one ground or the other.

The Courts below have negatived this contention solely on the basis that if an outsider is introduced as a Co sharer in a property it will make common management extremely difficult and destroy the benefits of ownership in common. [128F] 3.

The respondent No. 2, a Hindu widow, had two wives. The first wife was the adopted son of the second respondent by name Anand Babu. In February 1985, during the pendency of the special leave petition, the adoptive mother died. The respondents filed a suit for title and injunction. While each of the parties had taken such stand in the litigation a compromise was brought about on 21.8.1987 between the father and his two sons and the same was filed in this Court. The terms of the compromise stipulated payment of Rs. 1 lakh by the father to each of his two son in lieu of relinquishment of their interest. When the matter was listed before the Court for recording of the compromised, Sudarshan Gupta, second respondent maintained that he had not been paid Rs.1 lakh as stipulated and he had no intention to accept the compromise. The alienees have now been brought on record unders order of this Court, which is in accord with the principle indicated in the said decision and are of the view that as the compromise petition is genuine and lawful the same has to be acted upon. Allowing the special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The alienations are for about a purported consideration of Rs 4 lakhs. The sale deeds indicate that a sum of Rs, 1 lakh had been received earlier and a net amount of Rs 77,124 out of the consideration money under these documents has been paid before the registering authority. The transferees have admittedly been in possession of the property from the date of the sales which is more than three years old by now. Admittedly, the transfers are pendente lite. In fact if the compromise is valid and binding the alienor respondent No 2 had no interest in the property to part with in view of the stipulation in the compromise that on receipt of Rs 1 lakh he relinquished his entire interest in it. The alienation has made an attempt to hold out that there were agreements for sale prior to the compromise for which there is no acceptable evidence. [541D E] 2. The transferee had no right created under the alleged sale deeds. Their possession is without authority of law. Ordinarily, they would have been liable to account for mesne profits. In view of this fact that there was the allegation of payment of money by the alienees. He sought to rely on certain decisions which on being referred to were found to be totally inapplicable to the facts of the case. On the other hand, it is found that a similar question arose before the Orissa High Court in the case of Bhoja Govinda Maikap & Anr. vs Janaki Dei & Ors., AIR (1980) Ori. 108 where the power of the court under Order 23, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the face of an objection of one of the party to the compromised was considered.

The workmen of the appellant company, who were workers in the respondent 's industry, claimed that they were entitled to the sickness benefit for the first two days of sickness except in the case of a spell of sickness following, at an interval of not more than 15 days, the spell of illness for which sickness benefit was last paid. The workmen also felt aggrieved because by virtue of the first proviso to section 49 of the , they were not entitled to sickness benefit under the scheme of the Act. The company resisted both the cases on the ground that the benefits of sections 47 and 49 of tile Act were already admissible to workmen in Baroda with effect from December 14, 1969, and they were quite adequate, the Tribunal committed an error of law in granting the additional benefits mentioned above. Allowing the appeals by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The scheme of benefits admissible under the Act cannot be said to cover the work men 's demand for sick leave to the extent allowed by the Tribunal. [83C] 2.1 In providing for periodical payments to an insured worker in case of sickness (sickness benefit) or for medical treatment or attendance to him or the members of his family, the legislature did not intend to substitute any of these benefits for the workmen 's right to get leave on full pay on the grounds of sickness. [86D] 2:2 The Tribunal was, therefore, justified in its view that the workmen are entitled to 7 days sick leave with wages on pro duction of a medical certificate. [87E F] 3.1 The benefit of sick leave has been allowed to the workmen of those companies. It would thus appear that the appellants have not been able to show that the awards in question were illegal or unjust; or would adversely affect the economy or the indus trial peace, or lead to imbalance in the conditions of service in other industrial establishments. [888A] 3:3 The Tribunal has examined this aspect of the controversy also and given adequate reasons for allowing the benefit of 7 days Sick leave in the manner set out in the award. Such a leave could not be categorised as privilege leave as, by its very nature, it would be admissible only in the cases of actual sickness certified by a registered medical practitioner. It will thus appear from the record that even though the Act was applicable to the workers of the Precision Bearings India Ltd., Baroda, Hindustan Brown Bovari Ltd., and M.S. University Press, Baroda, the benefit could not b.e said to be adequate for it works out to about half the average wage of a workman, and even that amount is not admissible for the 1st two days ' of sickness excepting in the ease of a period of sickness certified at an intervals of not less than 15 day, the period of illness would be very much beyond the paying capacity of the industry. [898B C] 4:4 The Tribunal had examined this question also and gave adequate reasons to allow the benefit to the sick leave. [90C] 5. In the instant case, the appellants had not been unable to show any reason to disagree with the view which it has taken. As has been stated, the Act came into force in the region concerned on December 14. 1969, till then it was the practice in the glass industries to grant sick leave without wages for periods varying from 6 to 10 days. [91G] 6:5 The Tribunal could not therefore be said that to have erred in restoring the benefit which the workmen were re ceiving under the award of 1958, for it was taken away under the mistaken impression that it had been adequately replaced by the new provisions on the coming into force of the .

The appellant was detained under the , by an order of detention passed on the 8th June, 1955. The grounds of detention were served on him along with the order of his detention. He challenged the validity of the order based on the ground that the detaining authority acted merely at the instance of the police who were in league with the Goan National Movement and to take up professionally the cause of persons in the position of Carlos. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The obligation to furnish particulars and duty to consider whether the disclosure of any facts involved therein is against public interest cannot be so exercised as to nullify the constitutional right of representation and an obligation to communicate cannot be implied in these circumstances. It was not necessary for the detaining authorities to have felt that the grounds furnished were so vague as to hamper him in his right to make a representation under article 22(5) and section 7 of the Act. The necessity for such a communication would arise only if the detenue, feeling the grounds to be vague, asks for particulars. But in the absence of any such request by the detenue the non communication of the decision cannot be held to have hampered his constitutional right Of representation and the obligation to supply particulars and the duty to considered whether the disclosed of any fact involved therein was against public interests. The requirement for such communication would depend on the facts of each case. In the present case there is no merit in this contention. (ii)The order of preventive detention was made without any real application of mind by the detaining Authority, that the authority acted only at the behest of the Police who were not in lete with the DeSte but also at the time of filing the affidavit. The fact that be bad made no such application for particulars is therefore a circumstance which may well be taken into consideration, in deciding whether the grounds can be considered to be invalid. (iii)The requirement for making a representation against his detention cannot be said to have been hampered by the non supply of particulars and failure to furnish the duty and to consider the sufficiency of such particulars would not vitiate the order.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre, Secundrabad. It was alleged that on April 4, 1958 he committed acts of gross misconduct. The allegations were as follows : "Knowing Kumari Prakash as the daughter of a brother Officer, Rao assisted her in going away from her parents protection and planning to run away with a sepoy. " He then took her in his scooter to the unit lines of 51 1 Gurkha Rifles where he arranged her meeting with a tea shop nearby where she received a present of sari and blouse from the sepoys in his presence. " The respondent was charged under section 120B, I.P.C., for having committed acts which were gross misconduct and as such dismissed from service. The Central Government found it to be unsatisfactory and on April 9, 1959 an order was passed removing the respondent from service by the appellant. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from service on the ground that r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954, was ultra vires the . The High Court allowed the petition holding that r, 14 of Army Rules was ultra rites and that the action taken thereunder was without any authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the words "subject to the provisions of this Act" occurring in section 19 makes section 19 subject to section 45 and the Central Government had thus no power to remove a person from the service in derogation of the provisions Of section 45. HELD : The power under section 19 is an independent power. Although section 19 uses the words 'subject to . , it speaks of removal of a personfrom the service. Section 45 provides that on conviction by court martial an officer is liable to be cashiered or to suffer such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned. For removal from the serv ice under section19 of the read with r.14 of the . Rules, the Central government may remove a "person from the Service". Rule 14 is such a rule : it is not ultra vires. It is not correct to say that there should be rules and subject to the provision of the Act and such rules, the C. Government may dismiss or remove from the services any person subject to this Act.

The appellant was a Panchayat under the C.P. & Berar Panchayat Act, 1946. On June 1, 1959, the Bombay Village Panchayat Act 1958 (Bombay Act III of 1959) came into effect in Vidharba region and by virtue of this Act the appellant was deemed to be a Panchayat. On July 14, 1961, the Panchayat passed resolution No. 2 with a view to levy octroi duty. The resolution further stated that the appellant 's appeal to the Standing Committee was rejected on September 4, 1963. Thereafter, the appellant filed an appeal before the Standing committee under section 124(5) of the Act before the Panchayat Samiti, Parseoni. The Standing Committee allowed the appeal of the Company on two grounds: (1) that it was necessary for the Panchayat to have the octroi limits fixed with the approval of the Collector before levying octroi under r. 21; and (2) that the approval was given by the Collector on January 14, 1964 relating back to April 1, 1963, and therefore the levy of octroi from April 1. 1963 was regularised. The appellant contended that r. 5 of the Fees Rules was ultra vires the powers of the rule making authority. Held:(i) The Standing committee inspected the premises of the company but in their order they have given very scanty facts, They do not say whether the tea is crushed, processed or treated chemically to convert it into a marketable commodity. (ii) Rule 5 of Rules framed under section 176(2)(XV) of C. P.C., does not require the Panchayat concerned to fix the octroi limit in the resolution passed under r .3(a). It only deals with two items, namely, (1 ) selection of the tax and the rate at which it is to be levied; and the rates at which the tax or fee to be imposed and the amount at which a tax is to levied. The inhabitants of the village would be entitled to object only to these two matters, namely (a) the tax, or fee imposed and (b) the rate. But the learned counsel for the appellant contended (i) that r . 5 was ultra rites as it had failed to fix octroi limits in accordance with law; (ii). that the Standing Committees were entitled to deal with the appeal on merits; (iii) that there was no proper publication under r, 4 of the Rules was announced by beat of drum in the village and (iv) that in any event the Collector could regularise an imposition made without the authority of law.
