The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the , on the ground that he 's activities were prejudicial to maintenance of public order. The grounds of detention stated as follows: 1. On 24.12.1985, between 10 and 10.30 A.M., the subject alongwith Ramashish Bangali, Gulam Rambriksha armed with Rifle, gun etc. came in car No. BHG 9372 on Katras Coal Dump and started indiscriminate firing to kill Birendra Pratap Singh a rival of his calendestine business of coal to establish his criminal superiority in full view of the shopkeepers, customers and passers by of the area. The petitioner/appellant made representation on 22nd January, 1986 and the appellant was informed that the said representation was rejected. Thereafter, the petitioner 's matter was referred to the Advisory Board. The order of detention was passed on an incident relating to exchange of fire between two rival groups. A criminal case had been registered in relation to the said incident pursuant to which the petitioner was already in custody. The detention order though dated 2nd January 1986 was served on or about 11th January,1986, it was served only on or after 11th February, 1986. It is the case of the petitioner that the detenu was not served with all the documents referred to and/or relied on. The detenu was served with the order of approval of the said order of his detention by the Government of Bihar. The appellant/petitioner contended that the order could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order was necessary for putting him back in jail. Allowing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1(a) The power of directing preventive detention given to the appropriate authorities must be exercised in exceptional cases as contemplated by the various provisions of the different statutes dealing with preventive detention and should be used with great deal of circumspection. There must be awareness of the facts necessitating preventive custody of a person for social defence. If a man is in custody and there is no imminent possibility of his being released, the power of preventive detention should not be exercised. [908C D] (b) The order dated 2.1.1986 was served upon the detenu on or before 11th of January, 1987. It does not appear that either the prospect of immediate release of the detenu or other factors which can justify the detention of a man in detention were properly considered in the light of the principles noted in the aforesaid decision and especially in Rameshwar Shaw vs District Magistrate, Burdwan & Anr., ; and Ramesh Yadav vs District Magis trate Etah & Ors., W.P. (Crl.) No. 2 96/86 dt 25.9.86 and Raj Kumar Singh vs The State of Bihar & Ors. Crl A. 353/86 with W. P. (crl) 27/86 dated 26th September, 1986, referred to. (c) In the instant case, when the actual order of deten tion was served against the detenu, the detenu had already surrendered in respect of the criminal charge against him. At the relevant time, the appellant/ petitioner was undertrial in the said criminal case. There is no indication that this factor or the question that the impugned detenu might be released or that there was such a possibility of release, was taken into consideration by the detaining Authority properly and seriously before the service of the order. [09D E] (d) The grounds for forming the satisfaction for the need for the detention were there, and there was rational nexus between the object of the Order as contemplated under the Act and the materials on record. The principles applicable in these types of preventive Detention cases have been discussed in the decisions of Suraj Pal Sahu vs State of Maharasthra & Ors, W. (Cr.) No 2 96 of 1986 with SLP (Crl) No.

Section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power upon the Administrator with the result that the licensed dealer is at his mercy while seeking permission to carry on money lending or banking business on the security of any article, ornament or both in the same premises in which he carried on business as such dealer. The High Court struck down sec. 28 only on the ground that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred on the Administrator to refuse permission or grant permission should be exercised and that the section confers an unguided, uncanalised and uncanalalised power without any criteria for guiding the discretion of the Administrator. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Union of India that sec.28 is part and parcel of the entire scheme of Gold Control as envisaged by the Act and the object of the enactment and the scheme affords sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The policy and the Scheme of the Act together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the , afford more than sufficient guidance in the matters of exercising the power of discretion conferred on him under sec. In fact, sec. 5(1) requires that the Administrator should have regard to the policy and purposes of the .Act in making his orders. Moreover against his order under that Sec a revision lies to Central Government which implies that he will have to make judicious use of his power or discretion and any improper exercise is liable to be corrected by a higher authority. If that be so it cannot be said that unfettered or uncanalised or arbitrary power has been conferred upon the Administration under sec . Moreover, regard must be had to be the nature of the restrictions imposed by the section. [955C D] Harakchand Ratanchand Banthias vs Asst. Collector of Central Excise Poona, II Division while declaring unamended sec. 27(6) in several of its clauses referred to certain concepts which Administrator was required to take into account, and these concepts were regarded as indefinite, uncertain and vague.

The properties involved in the suit consist of agricultural lands situated in Eragudi village, Musiri Taluk, Tiruchirappalli district. According to the appellants, the said lands had been granted in Inam to the ancestor of one Ambalathadum Pachai Kandai Udayavaravar Temple by the Carnatic Rulers before the advent of British power in India. The original grant deeds were not available; but at the time of settlement of the Inams in sixties of the last century, Inam title deeds were issued in favour of the family of Pachathai Kandi Udayaravar Temple at Eravudi village. The appellants averred that the properties covered by the grant bad been granted to the original grantee burdened with the obligation of performing certain services in a Matam; and that the said properties had been alienated from time to time, and as a result of the first alienation, the appellants became entitled to them. The trial Judge examined the whole evidence and came to the conclusion that the grant of the Inam was a personal inam and that it was not a grant in favour Of the religious endowment within the meaning of the Act. On appeal by the respondents, the lower appellate Court reversed the finding of the lower Appellate Court that the existence of the temple had not been proved; but held that the appellants had proved their title to the suit properties. The High Court also took the view that the question as to whether on facts proved in this case an inference can be drawn that the previous manager or trustee had been removed from office by other persons who were acting as de facto managers of a temple de facto, has not been discussed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that article 134 B would not apply to the present case because the alienations evidenced by Exts. A 3, A 6 and A 12 show that the alienors purported to transfer the properties not as Poojaris or managers of any temple but in their individual character as owners of the said property. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The question whether a transfer effected by the manager of a Hindu religious endowment on the basis that it belongs to him and not to the religious endowments, is irrelevant for the purpose of article 134B if it is shown to have been made on the foundation that the transferor treated the properties as his own, it does appear that the two earlier Privy Council decisions in Gnanasambanda 's case lend some support to the contention. (2) The character of the representations made by the previous managers in regard to their relation with the property which is the subject matter of transfer, is relevant for the purposes of article134 B.

The appellant, a partnership firm consisting of himself and the two persons aforementioned, applied to the District Magistrate for permission to construct a modern cinema theatre in a plot of land which he proposed to take on lease in Gandhi Nagar, Jammu. The application was rejected by the District Judge as per his order dated December 29, 1977. The State Government thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the legality and validity of the orders passed by the district Magistrate and the appellate authority namely, the State Government. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the licensing authority had no power under the Act or the Rules to make such an order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that even though the licence had originally been issued in the name of Ved Gupta, the right of operation of the licence has become the property of the firm by virtue of clauses 13 and 18 of the partnership deed and since Ved Gupta had been expelled from the partnership and had thereby ceased to be connected with the firm, he did not have the possession of the premises and he was not entitled to claim a renewal of the license. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The view taken by the learned Single Judge that the licence granted by the licensing authorities in favour of the Apsara Theatre was in favour to his individual capacity and he alone was the licensee, is erroneous. [581F] 2.1 In the light of the foregoing discussion, it is wholly unnecessary to deal with the reasons stated by the Acting Chief Justice in support of his conclusion that the impugned order was violative of principles of natural justice. The only other reason stated by him for quashing the District Magis trate 's order is that the District and Sessions Judge, Jammu had no jurisdiction or power to suspend the licence of the Theatre under any other circumstances. [583G] 2:2 It is now relevant to recall that what has happened in this case is that in a suit filed by Krishan Kumar along with 11 others, an order of temporary injunction was issued on September 23, 1980 restraining Ved Gupta from interfering in any manner with the running of the Cinema Theatre by the plaintiffs. Quite understandably, Ved Gupta on receipt of the order of permanent injunction informed the District magistrate by his letter dated September 24, 1980 that as a result of the said order, it had become impossible for him, for the time being to operate the cinema licence with effect from the date of the aforesaid letter and that he may be absolved from any liability for prosecution or any other action in law in the capacity of the licensee of the cinema in the event of any illegal act or offence being committed by others in the Cinema premises. On September 26, 1980, the Superintendent of Police, Jammu reported to the State District Magistrate that cinema exhibition in Apsa Theatre was being conducted by some persons other than the licensee and the police had challaned the licensee under section 6 of the Act. The District Magistrate was requested by the said letter that exhibition of cinematographs in the Theatre may be suspended till the final decision was rendered by the Court in favour either of the parties. It is not known how it can be said on the facts and circumstances of the case that the order passed by him directing the suspension of cinema shows in the theatre cannot be said to have visited the writ petitioners with any adverse civil consequences. They had no legal right whatever to conduct the cinema show in the cinema Theatre without a licence in contravention of the law. [584C E] 2 :3 The impugned order is not one suspending the licence issued in respect of the Dpsara Cinema by persons other then the licensee.

The respondent entered into an agreement with the appellants, of a composite character consisting of three distinct matters. There was also a clause for referring the disputes between the parties to arbitration. The appellants were put in possession of the mills and the factory on 31 8 1952. On 12 2 1954 the respondent issued a notice to the appellants calling upon them to show cause why the lease should not be cancelled and why they should not he evicted. The notice then went on to state that the respondent considered it necessary to issue certain directions for the "preservation of the demised premises and the goods and stock in trade etc., lying in the demised Premises" and the appellants were accordingly required not to remove the stock or raise any money on the security thereof, and to send daily reports to the Custodian. The respondent contended that he had no auth ority to issue the notice in question under section 12 of the Act. Held, that the power could be exercised only so as to override a bar imposed by any law but not the contract under which the lease is held, and this result flows according to him from the language of the non obstante clause which is limited to anything contained in any other law for the time being in force". The respondent was acting within his authority in issuing Exhibit C in so far as it concerned the lease granted in favour of the appellants. It was next contended that even if the Custodian had the power under section 10 to cancel the lease in favour Of the appellants he could be bad no power under that section to cancel a lease granted by himself and not by the evacuee.

The appellant, a minor son of Raghubir Singh, was born to Raghubir Singh on 14th March, 1963 and was only 13 years of age when the ceiling proceedings were finalised by the Sub Divisional Officer on 5th May, 1976. He further held that the provisions of the old ceiling law applied to the case but the Sub division Officer had committed an error of law in determining the ceiling area under the new law i.e. the Act of 1955. The Board went on to hold that there was no provision for separate units in Chapter III B of the Act, of 1955 and the applicant Raghubir Singh and his son Surendrapal Singh constituted one unit and not two units and the case was remanded to Sub Divisional officer, Hanumangarh, for fresh determination of the calling area for Raghubir Singh. Before the Division Bench of the High Court in the writ petitions it was urged on behalf of Raghubir singh that the power of general superintendence and control over all revenue courts vested in the Board could not be exercised to the detriment of the writ petitioners much less by way of suo motu exercise of powers. The High Court held that there is no provision in Chapter II B of Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 and that the Board of Revenue had appellate jurisdiction and it could not, therefore, make use of its powers of superintendence and Control and the order of the Board. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1. Section 221 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Rules, 1955 is similar to section 107 of the Government of India Act, 1915 in the Act. [728G] 2. The power is there, and it may be exercised sparingly in extraordinary case where interest of justice requires that the board should exercise the power. Under section 107, the Government has general powers of supervision and control of all revenue Courts. It is both administrative as well judicial powers. It was open to the Board to exercise its powers on all its subordinate courts in order to regulate the functioning of subordinate courts so as to keep them within their respective spheres of jurisdiction. If the subordinate court disregards any specific provision of law and does something illegal it is open to it to the board of Revenue to interfere and set the matter right. [628G H] 3. The appeal consequently fails and is dismissed with costs.

The first respondent, a journalist, was engaged in the production or publication of the said law reports. The first respondent filed an application before the Central Government under section 12 of the , praying for the benefits conferred upon him by the Act. The Central Government rejected the claim of the first respondent and held that the law reports published by it were not newspapers within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Act and that the demand made by the Deputy Labour Commissioner to comply with the order made by him on the basis of the recommendations of the Palekar Tribunal was unsustainable. The High Court accepted the plea of the Ist respondent and declared that the Law reports published were not newspaper as defined in the Act, and that they were not the newspapers within section 2 (b) and therefore the orders made by them were invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the two courts reports published in the law report were not presses but only newspaper reports which could be said to contain news so as to become newspaper. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The law reports which are being published by the Ist Respondent are newspapers and the employees employed by the first Respondent in their production or publishing of the law Reports should be extended the benefit of the orders passed by the Central Govern ment on the based on the recommendations made by Paleakar Award. [778C] 2. The expression "newspaper" is not defined in section 2 of the . The law report which are to be published by a newspaper and also comments on some of the recent decisions. Though the publication of these items by itself may not occupy a substantial part of a law report to make it a newspaper, the publication does not cease to be a newspaper within the definition of "new 'paper ' in the . [780E F] 3. The word "new" is used in the sense of "an journalist". It is not understood in the context of any particular case whether newspaper or newspaper is a newspaper. The term "newly closed" has been defined by section 2 to mean any person employed to do any work in, or in relation to, any newspaper establishment. [783G] 4. The definition of the expression "Newspaper ' is usually applied (except so far as concerns the important class of trade newspapers) to publications devoted mainly to recording current events and `periodicals ' to magazines, reviews, and journals which in so faras they are concerned with current events at all, are concerned to comment rather than to report; but newspapers merge into advertising sheets, periodicals into books and pamphlets and both into one another. [784C D] 5. The publication of items by themselves may not be a substantial portion of a newspaper report to making it a paper, but the publication is sufficient to make a law reports a newspaper which may after some time cease to he a newspaper or become a book of reference.

The appellant was a monthly tenant of the suit premises since about 2nd February, 1965. On or about 9th of February,1965 a fresh document of that date was executed and it is alleged that the licensor gave and granted his 'leave and licence ' to the licensee to use and occupy the said premises for the period of five years. Clause 2 of the agreement recites that the licensee had agreed to use the premises as above and merely for the purpose of workshop business. The period of leave and licence was to commence from 1st September, 1965 to 31st August, 1970 and it was further submitted that the appellant would be entitled to keep the keys of the said shop with him and shall be at liberty to work in the said Premises for twenty hours subject to restriction of rules and regulations imposed by the Municipal or any other local authority or authorities. The licensor had agreed that if he commits any default of any terms and conditions or fails to pay the compensation for two months or if the licensee at any time puts up false or adverse claim of tenancy or sub tenancy, the licensor shall be entitled 'to terminate the agreement and cancel and revoke the leave and license granted earlier and shall he entitled to take possession forthwith of the premises. It was further stipulated that the licence would be liable to be cancelled on the licensee surrendering possession of the demised premises by removing himself and his belongings on the expiry of the period for which the agreement or sooner termination or determination thereof after deducting all the dues if any for payment of compensation. The appellant filed a suit for eviction against the respondent on the ground that he was not a sub tenant as such or not, but only the subtenancy as such and therefore it was recorded that as agreed 'B.C. no preliminary issue was to be framed. The trial Judge in the instant case passed a decree in ejectment petition filed by the respondent and ordered the appellant to vacate the premises before 31st of January, 1975. Before the High Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent was not the owner of the workshop and also denied that he had given the workshop to him for conducting business. It is further contended that there was sub tenancy by the Respondent in favour of the appel lant as a monthly licensee of the business with the articles and machinery belonging to the appellant and not to the respondent, and that the agreement recited that the lessor was seized and possessed of and was otherwise well entitled as the monthly tenant. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In order to get the advantage of section 15A of the Bombay Rent Act, the occupant must be in occupation of the Premises as a licensee as defined in section 5(4A) on the 1st of February 1973. If he was such a licensee, the non obstante clause of section15A(1) give him the status and protection of a tenant in spite of there being anything to the contrary in any other law or in contract. But if he was so not a licensee under a subsisting agreement on the date of its filing. It would be construed not as a mere licence but as a lease. [1060C E] 1.2 In determining whether an agreement creates between the parties, the relationship of landlord and tenant or merely that of licensor and licensee the decisive consideration is the intention of the parties. Beopar Sahayak (P) Ltd. & Ors. vs Shri Vishwa Nath & 5 others, [1987] 2 Scale 27, held inapplicable.

The respondent was a resident of the former Dholpur State and the dispute which led to the suit related to a time before the merger of the erstwhile Dholpur Union into the Matsya Union. The case of the respondent was that in 1947 certain commodities including chuni with which appeal No. 887 was concerned could only be exported from the former Rajasthan State on export permits issued by the customs department of the said State. It was also the practice in that State that when permits for export were issued, export duties had to be paid in advance though the actual export was made later. Consequently, in June 1947, the respondent applied for and was granted a permit for export of 15,000 maunds of chuni, and in connection therewith he deposited Rs. 30,000/as export duty in advance. This permit had been granted on June 28, 1947 and remained in force upto December 2, 1947. Thereafter he could not export further as his permit was not extended. He could only export 4,572 maunds and 20 seers of chiuni before December 2. On May 15, 1949, the United State of Rajasthan was formed including the Matsaya Union into which the former State of Dholpur came to be merged in 1949 never recognised the obligations of the latter State unless it chose to recognise the obligation. The respondent 's case further was that though he asked the State for refund of this advance duty, the State did not pay back the same to him. In the meantime, rapid constitutional changes took place after August 15, 1947, by which all the old laws continued till they were repealed or altered, recognised that it was liable in the same way as would have been the merging State if there was any liability on the merged State. The suits were resisted by the State of Madhya Pradesh on various grounds; but the High Court dismissed them. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The new sovereign throughout this process of integration from 1948 to 1950 must be taken to have recognised the rights of the subjects and undertaken the liability, if any, of the old States. It follows therefore that the State would be liable under article 295(2) of the Constitution to meet the liabilities of all old States which eventually were included in it subject always to this that if the new State passed any law repealing the old law which would affect the liability or even otherwise that law would prevail and the liability may disappear provided the new law is within the competence of the State legislature and does not transgress the constitutional limitations after the Constitution came into force. (ii) The expression "Government of the corresponding Indian State" used in article 295 (2) would mean only the United state of Rajasthan as it was just before January 26, 1950 but also the old old laws which came to he merged into it through the process to which we have already referred.

The appellants were running a market as an occupation or business with high standards and that the notification directing the constitution of a Market Committee at Virudhunagar was an unreasonable restriction on their fundamental right to do business. The Act provided for the better regulation of buying and selling of commercial crops in the Presidency of Madras and for that purpose to establish markets and make rules for their proper administration. The appellants were not prevented from doing their business, but they challenged the validity of the provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. Held, that the impugned provisions of section 5 of the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act (Mad XX of 1933) were reasonable restrictions on a citizen 's right to carry on trade or business and the impugned provision was valid. The imposition of such restrictions was not unreasonable but amounted to an unreasonable restrictions on their right to hold property within the meaning of section 14 of the Indian Contract Act. The provisions of sections 107 and 108 of the said Act were reasonable restriction on a citizens 's rights to do trade, and therefore they were valid. Held further, that having regard to the entire scheme of the impugned Act, the impugned pro hibition of the appellants was not invalid as inconsistent with the provisions Of section 14. The impugned provisions were valid and did not contravene article 19(1)(f) or (g) of the Constitution. The contentions must fail. The contention that the appellants had really two fundamental rights: one is to carry out trade or 'business and the other is to hold their property, i.e., the market; that by reason of the notification they were not prohibited from holding the market as property, for they could still do business in the market established subject to the regulations and also do business outside the prescribed area ; and that they were therefore not prohibited by the Act was not a reasonable restriction within the terms of section 15 of the Contract Act and was invalid.

The appellants were convicted and sentenced to death by the Sessions judge. The High Court confirmed their convictions but reduced the sentence of imprisonment for life. Held, that section 377 of the Code of Criminal Procedure does not abrogate or modify that provision. It only saves the discretion of judges in this matter. In a case like that there is no special rule of evidence for this class of cases. But when appellate Judges disagree on the question of guilt differ on that of sentence it is usual not to impose the death penalty unless there are compelling reasons. The circumstances of each case cannot be used as a precedent to determine the conclusion on the facts in another case. All that is necessary is either to have direct proof of prior concert, or proof of circumstances which necessarily lead to that inference, or, as we prefer to put it in the time honoured way, "the incriminating facts must be incompatible with the innocence of the accused and incapable of explanation on any other reasonable hypothesis". The fact that the two accused were also there but they ran away together cannot be considered a ground for departing from this practice. In the present case there was no evidence of any prior meeting. There was no material to show that they ran apart at the same moment when discovered, but that they did not do so. The mere fact that they run away together would not make them liable under section 149 of the Indian Penal Code. The fact of their being in possession of a weapon which penetrates half an inch into the head is, in our opinion, sufficient to show the common intention of the appellants and the conviction was bad as no sentence could be passed unless two Judges concur because of section 377 Of the Code was imposed.

The petitioner was a Sub Inspector of Central Public Works Department under the Ministry of Works and Housing in Government of India. He was compulsorily retired by an order dated 3.8.1976 with effect from 5.11.76 made under Rule 56(j)(i) of Fundamental Rules. The petitioner challenged that order before the High Court on the ground that he was an officiating Sub Inspector in Class II service and was compulsorily retire by exercising the power under Rule 57(j) of the Fundamental Rules, as he had not at all been retired from service on 5.10.1976. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioner was an officer who was in Class I or Class II Service or post even when he held a post of either class substantively or temporarily or on officiating basis and therefore, on the date of the order he had completed the age of 54 years. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that as the petitioner had not attained the age Of 55 years by the date he had attained the maximum age of 50 years, he could have retired from serv ice with effect only from 5th November 1976 and, therefore, he cannot be deemed to have been compulsorily retired under sub clause (i). Dismissing the writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1. Rule 56 (j) is meant to cover only those who are in a post on a regular basis, i.e., in a substantive capacity, and not on an officiating basis only. [638C] 2. The possibility of a reversion to the substantive post is not germane to the exercise of power contained in F.R. 56(1)(i). The purpose of Fundamental Rule 56 is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire Government servant in the public interest and the classification of Government servants into two categories covered by sub clauses (i) and (ii) has a purpose behind it. If the condi tions indicated in sub clause(i) is satisfied, namely, the Government servant is in Class 1 or Class I service or post, the benefit must substantively belong to the two classes of service or posts cannot be introduced into the scheme. The purpose is to classify Gov ernment servants into three categories and sub cl.(i) takes within its sweep those Government servants who at the relevant time are in Class 11 service or on substantive basis. [625E F] 3.

The respondents filed a suit in the Subordinate Court of Masulipatam on 10th January, 1964. The deceased had filled a proposal for insurance for Rs. 50,000 on 27th December, 1960. There was medical examination by the doctor on the life of the deceased on 27st December,1960 and it was further alleged that the payment of the first premium would amount to acceptance of the proposal and advised the deceased to pay the first premiums in full. It was also stated that the said two cheques were encashed and the appellant had duly appropriated the amount and credited in the accounts towards the premium payable by the deceased. The Divisional Manager, Masulpatam Branch, denied liability on behalf of the appellant Corporation on 28th January 1961. Thereafter there was correspondence between the parties between 1st February, 1961 to 23rd December, 1963 wherein the respondents plaintiffs had claimed the payment and the appellants had denied liability for the same. On the 10th of January,1964, the respondents filed the suit in which it was alleged that there was a concluded and valid insurance contract between the deceased and the Corporation and that the insurance contracted commenced on 11th January. 1961 being the date of receipt of the balance towards premium by the Corporation. The Trial Court held that there is no concluded contract between them and the corporation, was untenable, according to the plaintiffs. It further noted that it was significant that the case set out in the plaint and the basis of the claim made in the notices sent to the Corporation was not that the proposal was as a matter of fact accepted by the Divisional Manager on the other hand, claim was that it should be deemed to have been accepted. Considering the evidence and the averments, the learned Subordinate Judge came to the conclusion that the accounts do not show the position alleged by the plaintiffs respondents that the amounts paid were appropriated towards the premiums and the Trial Court was of the opinion that the encashing of the cheques and the want of any further action to be done by the appellants did not themselves create a contract of insurance between the appellants and the respondent Corporation. On appeal, the High Court reversed the judgment and decree of the trial court dismissing the suit of the respondents. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in appreciating the facts and the evidence in this case. [353C] 2.1 In view of the fact that such a long time has elapsed and further in view of this fact that principal amount together with interest amounting to about Rs. 85,000/ have already been paid to the wife of the appellants, the Life Insurance Corporation in this ease does not insist on the full repayment of the sum paid and counsel on behalf for the Life insurance Corporation has stated that they would accept if half of what has been received by the respondents, namely principal together with Interest is paid back to the respondent. [356D E] 2:2 The mere receipt and retention of premium until after the death of the applicant or the mere preparation of the policy document is not acceptance. Acceptance must be signified by some act or acts agreed on by the parties or from which the law raises a presumption of acceptance. [357E F] MacGillivray & Parkington on Insurance Law, Seventh Edition p. 1267 at page 222 referred to. In this connection, the statement of law in Corpus Juris Secundum, Vol.

The appellants applied for an interim injunction restraining the Bank of India from taking any steps in pursuance of a letter of credit opened in favour of M/s. V.V. D.K. Cassim & Sons, which was the subject matter of the suit. The trial court granted an interim order restraining the bank from taking proceedings in pursuance thereof and remanded the suit for trial. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the order of the High Court amounted to a judgment or a decree and the expression "final order" in section 205(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935, meant a final decision on the rights of the parties in dispute in a suit or proceeding; and that the expression 'final order ' in section 109 Code of Civil Procedure means an interlocutory order passed by the Court of the rights and obligations of the party in dispute. HELD: The order refusing to grant interim injunction did not determine the rights, and obligations, of the respondents in relation to the matter in dispute, in the suit or proceedings from which appeal has arisen, was not final within the meaning of article 133(1)(a) and (b). [707 D] In the present case the order refusing an interim relief did not finally dispose of a suit. It was not a final order within the contemplation of article133(1), because, the plaintiff 's suit as a result of the order was disposed of by the order directing the filing of a complaint under section 205 read with section 114 I.P.C. [708 G H] Mohanlal Maganlal Thakkar vs State of Gujarat, ; and Mohanlal Magan Lal Thakkar vs The King, , referred to.

Rule 174 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 enjoins that when goods owned by one person are manufactured by another the information is required relating to the price at which the said manufacturer is selling the said goods and the person so authorised agrees to discharge all the liabili tities under the said Act and the rules made thereunder. The price at the factory gate was Rs.5, then in such a case the value would be Rs.30 being the value of the grey cloth plus the value for the job work done plus manufac turing profit and expenses. That would be the correct as sessable value. If the trader, who entrusts cotton or man made fabric to the processor for processing on job work basis, would give a declaration to the operator as to what would be his price at what he would be selling the processed goods in the market, that would be taken by the Excise authorities as the assessable value of processed fabric and excise duty would be charged to the farce on that basis provided that the declaration as to the prices at which he would he selling the processing goods in a market, would include only the price or deemed price at that which the processed fabric would leave the processor 's factory plus his profit. Rule 174 enjoins that where goods ownedby one person were manufactured by other, the information was required relating t o the price to which the aforesaid manufacturer is sell ing the said items and the persons so authorised agree to discharge any of the liablities under this Act and rules made there thereunder. In order to explain the position it is made clear by the following illustration: if the value or value of a grey cloth in the hands of the processor is Rs.20, and the value thereof of the job worked plus manufacturing profit and manufacturing expenses whatev er these may be, which will either be included in the price, at the Factory gate or deemed to be the price for the processed fabrics or fabric plus the ting profit and the manufacturing expenses but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. It is necessary to include the processor"s expenses, costs and charges plus profit, but it is not necessary to mention the trader 's profits who gets the fabrics processed processed, because those would be post manufacturing profits.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti, Loharu. He was confirmed in that post in course of time. On January 21, 1974 he was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis. On April 1, 1975 he was confirmed with effect from March 14, 1975. The appellant challenged his absorption on a lower post and filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed by the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that by reason of section 14(4) of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1961 the appellant was entitled to continue in service of the Panchayat on the same terms and conditions on which he was employed by the Panchayats Samiti until they were absorbed in Government service or retire in such manner as may be prescribed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appointment of the appellant to the post of a Head clerk in 1963, long before June 13, 1973, was not recognised and protected, despite the fact that such appointment was made after June 13 1973 when the Amending Act came into force. There is no substance in this contention. Even assuming for the purposes of argument that the right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant had the right, to appoint him to the posts of Head Clerk or on April 1. [738C D] 2. The fact that the appellant is promoted as Head Clerk in January 1974 or the further fact that he was appointed lawfully to the Post of a clerk and that he is appointed lawfully does not alter his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after July 13, 1972 when the amending Act came in force. [ 738E] 3. The order of the Government of Haryana notified the absorption of the appel lant as a Clerk though as stated earlier he was working as a head clerk in the Loharam Panchayat Samiti. He is therefore entitled to be absorbed in government service as a clerks in any event. But, as a result of the deletion of section 33 of the Act by the Amending act of 1973, the Panchayat Samitis were divested of their power to make appointments to the Panchayats. The Government of Punjab notified the absorbing of the appellants as a junior clerk on April l, 1975 or the other fact that they were appointed as Head Clerks on April1, 1975 cannot improve his position.

The appellants filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math Sauna or the deity Sri Thakur Gokarneshwar Mahadeo Ji installed in the Math. The suit was contested by the first defendant, Kedar Nath Chaubey, also referred to as Uma Shankar Yati. The High Court allowed both the appeals by its judgment and decree dated April 21, 1969. It held that the Amauli properties had been purchased by Mahant Shivshankar Yati for Rs. 40,000 forming part of a fund left behind by his predecessor Sri Mahant Shivpher Yati and that the income from the properties belonging to the math and deity left any appreciable surplus after meeting the expenditure on account of bhog, arpan deepdan daily and annual puja and other obligations specified in the waqf deed. The present appeal is directed against that part of the judgment and order of the High Court. It was contended for the appellants that where a nucleus of dedicated property exists, the acquisition of additional property should be attributed to the application of the nucleum and must, therefore, be regarded as property belonging to Math or the temple. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The fund from which the Amaiuli properties were acquired constituted the personal property of Mahant Shiv Shankar Yatati who in 1921 employed it for the purchase of the Amaul properties. Mahant Shiv Shanker Yati executed a will in 1956 and it appears beyond dispute that by virtue of this will the Amahi properties devolved on Uma ShankarYati. It is pointed out before us that in assessment proceedings under the U. P. Agriculture Income Tax Act 1948, the Amaoli properties were described by Mahant Sheo Shankar Yutti as properties of the Math and therefore a claim to exemption from the levy was made. The question whether the fund was the personal Property of Mahant or deity is the personal properties of Mahant, the burden of proof resting on the party who makes the claim. [663D E] 2. In assessment proceedings tinder the U P. Agricultural Income Tax, Act 1948 the Amaiii properties were mentioned by Mahant Sri Shiv ShankarYathas Yati as properties and of the math or deity. The income from these properties was not challenged by the plaintiffs in the present suit.

The appellants were displaced persons from West Pakistan. They applied for consolidation of their lands with those of the appellants in the village Raikot. During the pendency of this application he died and after his death, the application was continued by the appellants. The Additional Custodian cancelled the allotment of land in favour of the 14 allottees on the ground that the cancellation was a result of misapprehension of the actual facts and that they were not entitled to allotment of suburban lands at all. The appellants moved the Deputy Custodian for calling up their review application and for revising the order cancelling their allotments on the grounds that this cancellation was an outcome of misapprehension in the actual fact and that the appellants were not, entitled to allot of sub urban land at all; that consequently their allotment had been wrongly made but referred the matter back to the Additional Custodian for decision. The Deputy Custodian rejected the application on the view that r. 14(6) of the Evacuee Property Rules which came into force on July 22, 1952 stood in the way of cancellation of the allotment in favour Of the appellants and that consequently the allotment had already been cancelled earlier. On appeal by the appellant to the Custodian General the Additional Deputy Custodian held that his jurisdiction to revise the order had been taken away by virtue of the provisions of section 19(1) of 1954 and the notification issued thereunder on March 24, 1955. The revision application filed by the 14 appellants was dismissed by the Additional Commissioner on August 20, 1952. On December 17, 1954, the appellants moved a Deputy Custodian General for calling for review of his order cancelling the allotment on the same ground that this cancelled the allotments in their favour by the order dated October 31, 1952 and that therefore their allotment having been cancelled subsequently, they were entitled to the protection of section 10 of the Act. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the powers of the Custodian under the , to allot any property to a person or to cancel an allotment existing in favour could not be exercised by him as it was not based upon any of the grounds set out in the 6th condition and that r, 14(1), which came in force on 7th August 1949 stood in that way. Held, further, that the power of the custodian under section 12(2) to allot evacuee property to displaced persons by publishing in the official gazette a notification to the effect that it had decided to acquire such evacuee property in pursuance of this provision was not completely in conflict with section 10 and that there was no occasion for him to say anything about it. The power of cancellation conferred by section 19 of the 1954 Act on a managing officer or a managing corporation constituted under that Act is confined only to properties which are entrusted to them for management and not with respect to any other property. Section 17 deals with the functions; duties of managing officers and managing corporations.

The State Public Service Commission had undertaken the recruitment to the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Women) District Inspectress of Girls Schools/Associate Regional Inspectress of Schools in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (Women 's Branch) The advertisement inviting applications from eligible candidates was published on May 5, 1985 and a corrigendum was published in June 8, 1985. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examina tion was over, on the basis of the results thereof success ful candidates upto a base limit have to be called to be interviewed. On account of improper feeding into the comput er some of the candidates who had better performance in the written examination were not called and candidates securing lesser marks in the viva voce examination were selected. When this position was known and upon an inquiry was factually estab lished, the Public Service Com mission decided to cancel the entire recruitment examination and asked for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the ground that the written exami nation was over. The High Court upheld the action of the Public Services Commission and dismissed the writ petitions. In these appeals by special leave it was contended on behalf of the State that when no defect was pointed out in regard to the written test and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the Written examination from the interview, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examina tation. On the other hand, it was submitted on behalf the State Government that when there was a defect pointed out, there could be no justification to cancel that the oral part of tho recruitment exami nal and the only objection was limited to exclusion. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.

The appellant brought the suit on the allegation that there was one Shiromani Nirankari Dera at Patiala, that this institution had two branches one at Landeke in Moga Tehsil and the other at Nanga Kheri in the erstwhile Patiala State. The prayer in the plaint was for recovery of possession of the Dera and the properties attached to it. Som Dass, the defendant, contended that the Dhoh at Landake was an independent Dera, that he was in possession of those properties as its lawfully appointed mahant, that the appellant had no right to recover possession of these properties of the dera and entitled to manage the properties of Dera. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal by the defendant the decree was reversed. Against this decree an appeal was preferred by the appellant to the High Court. While the appeal was pending in the High court, Som Dass died on 13 10 1970. No application was made by the appel lant to bring on record his legal representatives within the period prescribed. An application was filed on 1 2 1971 by the plaintiff stating that Som Dass had died on 26 11 1970 leaving behind him Shiam Dass as his Chela and for impleading him, that Som Das, the respondent, who was the mahant of the said Dera should be impleaded as a party under Order 22, r. 10, of the Civil Procedure Code against the person upon whom the interest had devolved, and that the appe lant did not know about the death of Som Dass at the time he died. The High Court held that after the death Of Som Dass Shiam Das, Shiam Chand as his chela "inherited the sum total of the rights which earlier vested in Som Dass and when a controversy is raised about such rights, then the appellant was bound to bring the suit for the recovery of posses sion of the properties. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the respondent that there were no devolution of the interest in the subject matter of the suit, since there was no certainty as to the person who would be elected as mahant to succeed him. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The devolution of interest in a subject matter is taken place when Shiam Ram Dass was elected as Mahants of the temple after the demise of Som Das Dass. Som Das was sued in his capacity as a person who claimed (though illegally according to the appellant) as mahants of Dhogh and Som Dass was sued and as it was in the same representative capacity that the appeal is sought to be continued against Shiam Lal, Order 22 rule 10 would not be attracted. [489C] 2. The suit against Som Dass is not in his personal capacity but in his capacities as de facto mahant. In other words, the suit was for possession and management of the Eera and its properties and it devolved upon shiam Dass by virtue of his election as ma ties subsequent to the death. [490E F] 3. The word 'interest ' which is mentioned in this rule means interest in property i.e., the subject matters of the main suit and the interest is the interest of the person, who is the party to the suit.[490G H] 4. devolution of a interest in an estate cannot be brought to an end merely because the interest or of a party in the matter of suit has devolved upon another during the pendency of the litigation but that suit may be continued on the person acquiring the interest with the leave of the Court. When a suit is brought by or against a person in a representative capacity and there is a devolution of his interest, the rule that has to be applied is Order 22 Rule 10 and not rule 3 or 4, whether the devolution takes place as a consequence of death or for any other reason.

The Andhra Pradesh State and Karnataka had framed the Andhra Pradesh Civil Service (Classification, Control & Appeal) Rules, 1979. The validity of these rules was challenged by some of the petitioners who were working as Junior Engineers in the Andhra State. They contended that the age of retirement was increased from 55 to 58 years with effect from October 29, 1979 after an elaborate and scientific inquiry by a committee constituted under Rule 2 of the Andhra Civil Service Rules, and nothing had happened since then to justify reduction of the age. The Government of Andhra Pradesh rejected their claim for premature retirement on the ground that they were not competent to reduce their age. It was contended that there was no basis at all for reducing the age as it was arbitrary and unconnected with the object which it sought to achieve. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The power of the Governor under Article 309 is a legislative power and the Legislature has the power to make provision for removing the difficulty arising in the exercise of such power. [655E] 1.2 The Government had exercised its power arbitrarily without having regard to factors which are relevant on the fixation of the retirement age at 58. It is not arbitrary or unreasonable in the circumstances of the case. The recommendation of the Second Central Pay Commission that the retirement should be raised from 55 and that the said recommendation was accepted by the State Government and consequently, the age was raised to 58 with effect form the date of retirement. [557F G] 1:3. The fact that the decision to reduce the age is taken by the Government cannot justify the conclusion that it is arbitrary because it is unscientific in the sense that it was not backed by due investigation or by compilation of relevant data on the subject. If reduction of retirement age from 58 to 55 is to be regarded as arbitrary on the grounds that it overlooks the advance made in longevity, fixation of retirement at 58 is also not likely to sustain the charge of arbitrariness. [60G H] 1 :4. The question whether the exercise by the Governor of Andhra pradesh was arbitrary or irrational and unconnected to the object of the Act has to be kept out of consideration in so far as the question of the power of compulsory retirement is concerned. [61C D] 2.1 It is well settled that the power conferred on the Governor by Article 309 can be exercised only for good reasons and not for any other purpose. The power to retire a Government employee, not being a workman and not belonging to Last Grade Service, shall retire from service on the afternoon of the last day of the month in which he attains the are of 55 years. [62E F] 2:2 It is difficult to appreciate how the exercise undertaken by the High Court of power can be challenged as lacking in authority. The recommendations made by the Second Pay Commission were not accepted by Government initially because it felt that raising the age at 55 was a fair and reasonable basis. The report of the Commission has therefore to be treated as a valid exercise of legislative power.

The appellants are a registered dealer in the State of Haryana. He purchased certain raw materials in the state without paying tax thereon, in view of the provision contained in section 24 of the Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973. The assessee was not liable to pay the purchase tax on the raw materials imposed under section 9(1) of the Act. This claim has been rejected by the taxing authorities and the High Court and hence these appeals. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The purchases of raw materials by the assessees are goods on the sales of which tax is leviable under the Act though the assessees were exempt from payment of such tax by reason of section 24(1). [351G] 2. The definition also excludes from its purview "the sale proceeds of goods on which purchase tax is levied under this Act" and "the purchase value of any goods on tho sales of Which tax is payable under this act". There can be no dispute that a tax is impos ed under the statute on the goods in question when they are sold by a dealer and, indeed, the assessees would have had to pay tax on them. But let us examine what the position would be if we hold, as con tended by Shri Gupta, that the effect of the decision is that the words "or despatches the manufactured goods to a place outside the State in any manner otherwise than by way of sale in the course of inter State trade or commerce" in section 9 (1)(b) should be deemed to have been deleted from the statute. This definition includes within the definition of 'turnover ' the purchase value o f goods liable to tax under section 8 but, the goods presently in question are not laible to tax u/s 9(i) or section 6 or section 24 (3). [353C D] 3. The words "disposes of" used in clause (a)(ii) later, clause (b) also includes cases of despatches by a registered dealers of the manufactured candi dates outside the territory of India within the meaning of sub section (1)of section 5 of the Central Sales Tax. [353F] 4.

The appellant firm was registered under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. The goods were sent to the sellers by the sellers on board the ship and they were delivered to the buyers on board. The sellers returned the goods to the seller on the ground that these sales were not their property till the goods had crossed the customs barrier and thus entered the export stream. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the claim for exemption and assessed them to purchase tax under section 10(b) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act on the grounds that they remained the sellers ' property till they were brought on board and so the sales were exempted from tax under article 286(1)(b). The appellant 's appeal was dismissed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. In further appeals to the Tribunal, the High Court held that the goods remained the seller 's property till after they had crossed customs barrier, and that therefore the exemption under article286(1) will come into operation. Held, that the words " a person " in section 10 (b) are wide enough to include a registered dealer and an unregistered dealer. The words " the time of the export" mean the time when the goods cross the customs frontier. The word " a registered dealers" is wide enough and includes a registered firm. In the United Motors case, the goods were on shipped by the seller and the contract was that payment will be made on the presentation of the bill of lading. The contract being that payment would be made at the time the goods reached the destination, the purchasing dealer had the intention as stated and ultimately he sold to a registered person. The fact remains that the intention declared has not been carried out. Held further, that in view of the provisions of section 10 of the Act no purchase tax was leviable from them under article 285(1).

The respondent husband married the appellant wife as a second wife, way back in 1956 and a few years later had a son by her. The initial warmth vanished and the jealousies of a triangular situation erupted, marring mutual affection. The respondent divorced the appellant around July 1962. A suit relating to a flat in which the husband had housed the wife resulted in a consent decree which also settled the marital disputes. For instance it recited that this respondent had transferred the suit premises, namely, a flat, in Bombay, to the appellant and also the shares of the Cooperative Housing Society which built the flat concerned. There was a clause in the compromise that the appellant declares that she has now no claim or right whatsoever against the defendant or against the estate and the properties of the defendant. The appellant finding herself in financial straits and unable to maintain herself, moved the magistrate under section 125 Cr. P.C., 1973 for a monthly allowance for the maintenance of herself and her child. She proceeded on the footing that she was still a wife while the respondent rejected this status and asserted that she had been a divorcee. The Magistrate who tried the petition for maintenance held that the respondent was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 300/ for the son and Rs. 400/ for her subsistence taking due note of the fact that the cost of living in Bombay where the parties lived, was high, and that the Respondent had provided residential accommodation to the appel lant. This order was challenged before the Sessions Judge by the aggrieved husband who on a strange view of the law that the court under section 127 had no jurisdic tion to consider whether the applicant was a wife, dismissed the petition in allowance of the appeal. The High Court rejected the revision petition and summarily dismissed a revision petition. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the courts below had surprisingly forgotten the plain provision in the Explanation (b) to section 125(1) of the Code which provides that "wife ' includes a woman who has been divorced by or has obtained a divorce from her husband and has not remarried. On behalf of the respondent it was urged that the Courts below had strangely forgotten that the plain provisions in the explanation (b), set up anywhere in the courts, below or urged before them. The contention was apparently based upon contractual arrangement in the consent decree read with section 127(3) (b). Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The scheme of the complex of provi sions in Chapter IX has a social purpose. Ill used wives and desparate divorcees shall not be driven to material and moral dereliction to seek sanctuary in the streets. This traumatic horror animates the amplitude of section 127 (3) is dynamic and its meaning cannot he pedantic but purposeful. The proposition, therefore, is that no husband can claim under section 126(3)(b) absolution from this obligation under section125 towards a divorced wife except on proof of payment of a sum stipulated by customary or personal law whose quantum is more or less sufficient to do duty for maintenance allowance. [78C E] 1.2. The compulsive conclusion from a divorce by a husband and his provision of a separate residence as evidenced by the consent decrees fills the bill. Do divorcees have to 1) prove mutual consent to live apart; Divorce painfully implies that the husband orders her out of the conjugal home. If law has nexus with life this argument is still born. The last defence, based on meharhar payment merits more serious attention. The contractual limb of the contention must easily fail. [79D E] 2.1 In the normal course, an order for maintenance must follow, the quantum having been determined by the learned Magistrate at the trial level.

The appellant, a dealer in liquor shop, had bid for Rs.11,900 (Rupees eleven thousands only) per month Dak in an auction of Beni Country liquor shop held on 27.3.88 and he as given the shop of Beni country liquor but after signing in Bandobasti Register he did not deposit dak amount. The name of Shri Raghu Nath Thakur S/o Late Gorakh Nath Village Repura, P.S. Pusa, Distt. Samastipur was placed in the black list for future under the orders passed by the Collector, Samasti. This order was passed pursuant to the order of the Collector. The letter dated 25th March, 1988 stated that no notice had been given to the appellant of the proposal of black listing the appellant. It was contended on behalf of the State Government that there was no requirement in the rule of giving any prior notice before black listing any person. In so far as the contention that there is no requirement specifically of giving a prior notice is concerned, the respondent was right. But it was an implied principle of the rule that any order having civil consequence should be passed only after following the principles of natural justice. It has to be realised that black listing every person in respect of business ventures has civil consequence for the future business of the person concerned in any event. Even if the rules do not express so, it is an elementary principle of natural Justice that parties affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order. In this view of the matter, the last portion of the order in so far it directs black listing of the appellant in respect thereof cannot be sustained in law.

The property which was the subject matter of the dispute originally formed part of an extent of land situat ed on Mount Road, Madras bearing door Nos. 2 and 3 and a building thereon. The rent for the premises was Rs. 150 per month. On 30.7.1953 all the co owners of the property (includ ing G.G.) sold the property to the United India Life Assur ance Company and the New Guardian of India Life Insurance Company Ltd. In 1956, the Life Insurance Corporation of India stepped into the shoes of these two insurance companies and became the owner of the said property. On 20.7 .65, the LIC moved two applications (being HRC Nos. 3310 and 3311 of 1965) in the court of the Rent Controller (Sri A. Varadarajan who later became a Judge of this Court) for fixation of fair rent in respect of item No. 1 as against the rent of Rs.150 p.m. fixed under the lease deed. So far as item 2 was concerned, it appears that at the time of hearing it was conceded before the Rent controller that the respondents were tenants of the entire properties covered by the lease deeds and that they had not constructed any of the premises thereupon. The Rent Controller rejected these applications on the ground that since the subject matters of the lease under exhibit P 1 was only a vacant site, the Rent Control Authority had no juris diction to fix the fair rent. On appeal, the Court of Small Causes held that the buildings on the land leased under exhibit PW 1 had also been conveyed to the LIC and that the LIC was entitled to seek fixation offair rent in regard thereof and that, therefore, the claim in the suit for arrears of rent based on Rent Controller 's order in respect thereof had to fail. The petitioner was given an opportunity to file his objections to the preliminary list. The High Court of Mysore held that the writ petition was premature as the final list of officers on an integrated seniority list was still to be prepared after hearing objections. The petitioner, who had retired from service, filed a Writ Petition in this Court challenging the validity of the final gradation list. It was contended by him that he was not heard after the final seniority list had been prepared and that the rules had not been complied with. Dismissing the writ Petition, HELD: 1.1 The combined final gradation List dated April 6, 1962, so far as category 6 is concerned, is ultra vires and illegal and that part of the notification alone must be quashed by grant of a writ in the nature of certiorari. [829H; 830A] 1.2 In order to establish the invalidity of the provisional list on some such grounds of invalidity, those grounds have to be shown to exist. The Court cannot go into the merits or otherwise of equation of posts which is a matter within the province of the Central Government. It would, therefore, be quite fair to give a person affected an 'oppo opportunity to be heard against the proposed final gradation before it is finalised so that any possible mistakes, either on facts relating to his particular case or of law in applying the rules governing seniority to those facts, may be rectified. But once he has had that opportunity, it cannot possibly be said that he should have a further opportunity against even a final seniority List. If he was to have that opportunity the list would not really be final but only provisional or preliminary. It will be obviously contradictory to hold it to be a final list and yet declare it subject to modifica tions on further objections. [ 830E F] 1:3 The combined tentative gradation list dated April, 1962 so faras category 6 in respect of category 6 was concerned, was ultra vires as well as illegal and illegal.

The petitioners in both these writ petitions are partnership firms carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of polished diamonds. The Import & Export Policy for the period April 1978 to March, 1991 in para 174 of the Import & Exports Policy for April 1988 to March 1979 in para 215 made provision for grant of certain import facilities to Export Houses which were registered in accordance with the provisions of the said Policy. One of the conditions was that the Export House would be eligible to Additional Licences on the basis of the export actually made in preceding three licensing years termed as 'the Base period '. The petitioners submitted application for registration as Export Houses and for grant or renewal of Export House Certificate which would have entitled them to the grant of such Additional Licence. The said applications were rejected by the authorities on the view that they had failed to diversify their export of "Other products" during the year 1977 78. The order refusing the Export Certificate was challenged by the petitioners by filing writ petitions under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Bombay High Court which dismissed the same. While the said appeal and other writ petition (filed by the Petitioners viz. Writ Petition No. 460 of 1988) were pending in the Bombay, this Court decided Civil Appeal No. 1423 of 1984, Union of India vs Rajnikant Brothers, and other connected matters by order dated April 18, 1985 wherein it was observed that there was no requirement of diversification of exports as a condition for grant/ entitlement of Export Houses in the Import Policy for 1978 79 and the Export Houses who were issued Additional Licences prior to April 1, 1988, on the ground that they have failed to carry out their export obligations during the period 1977 78 in accordance therewith. The Court further directed the authorities to grant Export House Certificates to the petitioners under the Import and Export Policy 1978 79 within three months. While construing the aforesaid direction contained in its order dated 4th April, 1985 in Rajnarayanikant Brothers case (supra) this Court has held that the grantees of the Additional Licences were not only prohibited from importing items which were excluded under the Export Policy1978 79 but also from importing item excluded under Import Policy prevailing at the time of import and that the word 'banned ' was intended to take in terms which were banned altogether as well as items which are `non canalised ' and also item which are 'canalised ' could not be ruled out and it was in this light that the Court can be said to have used the words "whether canalised or otherwise ' contained in the order dated 1st April, 1988. The High Court further held that under Import & export Policy 197879 Additional licences were to be given on the basic basis of one third of the f.o.b. value of the exports made in 1977 78 whereas under Import and export policy 1988 91 Additional Licences are to be granted on the same basis as permissible during the licensing year to which the application pertains, but the items to be allowed will be as per the Import policy in force on the date of issue of the licence. The grievance of the petitioners is confined to sub para (10) of para 218 which lays down that Additional licences issued to Export House/Trading Houses prior to 1st March, 1988 shall cease to be valid for import of items of raw materials, components and consumables covered by Appendices 3 and 5 Part A and items of non OGL capital goods (other than those covered by Appendix 1 Part A) and items available under this Policy.
