The appellant was an Accountant cum Head Clerk in the Tamil Nadu Forest Training School at Vaigai Dam. He took charge of the office on 6.10.1975 and had been residing in a house opposite the training school. PW 3, the Principal of the training School issued exhibit P 2 show cause notice to the PW 1, Venkataswamy, the canteen contractor as to why his licence for running the canteen should not be cancelled. This was on the basis of a complaint made by the appellant that the food served in the canteen was substand ard. The appellant produced the currency notes. PW 6 conducted the phenolphthalein test with reference to the fingers of the appellant. The test was positive, the currency note were seized and the appellant arrested. At the trial, the prosecution witnesses supported the case. PW 1 affirmed the fact that the appellant made the demand and had also received the amount on 22.10 .1975 itself passed orders and closed the file. The Trial Court accepted the prosecution evidence, rejected the plea of the appel lant and recorded the conviction. Before this Court it was contended for the appellant: (i) that there was no independent evidence regarding the demand, the messenger who had contacted PW 1 at the behest of the accused had not been examined; (ii) that the conviction under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act is to be maintained, no separate sentence need be award ed under section161 I. P.C.; (iii) that even though the conviction was under section 165 I.I.P., and section5(2), of the Act is not attracted on the proved facts is also not impressive; and (iv) that it was highly improbable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The prosecution has failed to prove the guilt of the appellants in view of the presumption arising under section 4(1) of Prevention of Corrup tion Act which has not been rebutted. [337F] 2. The conviction cannot therefore be sustained. [340C] 3. The burden resting on the accused person in such a case would not be as light as it is where a presumption is raised under section 114 of Evidence Act and cannot be held to be discharged merely by reason of the fact of that the explanation offered by the accused is reasonable and probable. It must further be shown that the Explanation is a true one. The words 'unless the contrary is proved ' which occur in this provision make it clear that the presumption has to be rebutted by 'proof ' and not by a bare explanation which is merely plausible. A fact is said to be proved when its existence is directly established or when upon the material before it the Court finds its existence to be so probable that a reasonable man would act on the supposition that it exists. Unless, there fore, the explanation is supported by proof, the presumption created by the provision cannot be said to ' be rebutted. On a careful consideration of the facts and circum stances, this court is not satisfied that the appe lant had even by preponderance of probability succeeded in rebutting the presumption. [341E F] 4.

The petitioner was an Under Secretary to the Government of India in the Ministry of Shipping and Transport and on May 21, 1974 accepted employment as Joint Manager in the Mogul Line Limited, a Government of india undertaking after obtaining release from government service. He was first allotted a service quarter. In 1975 the company purchased a spacious flat being flat No. 151 in Jolly Maker apartment III at 119 Cuffe Parade and the petitioner being the senior most executive was allotted the flat for his residence. The petitioner retired from the service of the company on or about September 30, 1984. Prior to that i.e. On September 26, 1984 he addressed a letter requesting the company to permit him to continue to live in the company 's premises during the period of his accumulated leave after his retirement and in accordance with the company rules, he was required to pay compensation for the use of the premises. After the expiry of the said period of six months, the company addressed a letters requesting the petitioner to vacate the flat stating that if he failed to do so, he would be liable to pay higher compensation as per the company"s rules. Since the petitioner failed to vacate, the Company initiated proceedings for his eviction under the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised occupants) Act, 1971. The Estate Officer by order dated December 2, 1985 directed the eviction of the petitioner. The Petitioner filed a suit in the Court of Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate 37th Court Esplanade, Bombay alleging that he was wrongfully withholding the flat in question which had been given to him for his own residence during the periods of his employment and thereby committed an offence punishable under section 630 of the Act. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the view expressed by the Single Judge following the earlier decisions of the High Court in Amritlal Chum vs Devi Devi Ranjan Ranjan Ranjan Jha, ; , that it refers only to the existing officers and employees of a company within the ambit of section 630 was limited to such property of the Company which was wrongfully obtained by an officer or employee of the companies. The High Court dismissed the special leave petition filed by the petitioner under Article 226 of the Constitution and held that the construction placed by the High court on the provisions contained in section 630(1) of the is the only construction possible construction possible. In the Special Leave Petition it was contended for the petitioner that the provision contained in Section 630 of tho Act is a penal provision and therefore must be subject to a strict construction and there is no room for intendment. It was further submitted that on a true construction, the scope and effect of the section was limited only to such properties of the Companies which was illegally obtained by the officer or employees of the firm and not to those whose employment has been terminated. The beneficent provision contained therein in Section 630(1), namely, where an officer and employee of a Company wrongfully withholds possession of property of a public company, or (b) having obtained such property during the course of his employ, to which he is not entitled; and that both clauses (a) and (b), are separated by the word 'or ' and therefore are clearly disjunctive.

The deity of his worship was Shri Vithal Rukhamai Sansthan. Though the origin of the Sansthan is dipped somewhat in antiquity and direct testimony was lacking, it has never been disputed that Sakharam Maharaj constructed a temple in the year 1817 at Amalner and installed the aforesaid deity according to religious rites. He also acquired certain properties and the said temple with the properties constituted Shri Vithalrao Deshmukh of Amalerner. The sansthan had movable property of the value of Rs. 19,164/ and immovable properties of the values of Rs, 1,06,000/ and the average gross annual income as well as the average annual expenditure was Rs. 11,000 / . After passing of the Bombay Public Trusts Act 1950 (No. 29 of 1950) an application under section 18 of that Act was filed by three persons Bhaskarrao Chimanrao Deshmukh, Ramrao Sahebrao Deshmukh and Ramkrishna Tryambak Deshpande, as constituted attorneys of Vasudeobuwa who was described in the application as the "owner" of the property. The word 'Buwa means saint. The application was made on May 29, 1952 to the Assistant Charity Commissioner, Poona under protest and without prejudice to the claim made therein that the Sansthan was not a public trust. In view of the penal provision under section 66 of the Act in the case of non compliance with section 18(1) of the said Act, the said application was filed ex abundanti cautela. The Assistant Charity Commis sioner after requisite notice made an enquiry into the matter in accordance with the provisions of the . On behalf of the applicants representing the Sansthan evidence of the attorney Ramkrishna Deshpande was recorded and he was cross examined by the assessors as well by the Assistant Commissioner. Some documents were also produced on behalf of them. The District Judge reversed the decision of the Charity Commissioner by his order dated October 16, 1959 and declared the Sansthan to be a private property and not a 'public trust '. The High Court set aside the order of the District Judge and restored that of the Deputy Charity Commissioner. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf Of the applicants: (1) that there is absolutely no evidence in this case about dedication to the public or public user of the temple as a matter of right; (2) that the High Court failed to consider all the material documents filed on behalf by the appellant except exhibit 35 and that the conclusion was highly erroneous being contrary to the one that had been reached by the District judge on appraisal of the entire documentary evidence. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (i) It is not always possible to have all the features of a public Trust in a given case. Even some of the tests laid down by this Court may be sufficient to enable the court to come to a conclusion about the character of the trust on documentary evidence, if any, the object and purpose for which the trust was created, the consistent manner in which the property has been dealt with or managed by those in charge, the manner in Which the property had long been used by the public, the contribution of the public to all intents and purposes, as a matters of right without the least interference or restriction from the temple authorities, to foster maintenance of the worship the accretion to the trust property by way of grants from the state of gifts from outsiders inconsistent with the private nature of the endowment, the nature of devolution of the properties, are all important elements in determination of the question whether a property is a 'private or a public religious endowment. [521 C E] (ii) It has been held that when property is dedicated for the worship of a family idol it is a private and not as a public endowment, as the persons who are entitled to worship at the shrine of the deity can only be the members of the family, and that is an ascertained group of individuals.

The assessee was assessed to income tax for the years 1943 44 to 1947 1948 and 1951 52 by the Third Income tax Officer, C. 1 Ward Bombay, at and for Rs. 40,178 4 0. The assessee not having paid up the assessed amount of tax the Income tax officer on the 10th April 1951 issued a warrant of arrest under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 requiring the assessee to appear before him in person on the 16th June 1955 and show cause why he should not be apprehended and confined to civil jail in satisfaction of the said certified demand. The sale proclamation was held on the 25th February 1955 fetching a price of Rs. 33,000 and it was confirmed on the 30th March 1955. The sales proclamation was issued on the 15th January 1955. On the 16st June 1955 an application was made by the present petitioner to the Bombay High Court under article 226 for quashing the said order. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that section 46(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 offends article 14 of the Constitution and that article 21 and article 14 were not void under article 13(1). On appeal by special leave: Held, that the law impugned before this Court has only adopted for its own purpose, the same coercive process which was devised by the States for their own purposes which are closely akin or similar to the purpose of the Union. The law was not dead and could not be assailed as repugnant to article 14 Of the Constitution. It was not correct to say that all the provisions of all the State laws for recovery of arrears of land revenue had been referentially incorporated in section 46 (2) at the time it was enacted to be treated as crystallised and to be applied by the Collectors, although the State law laws for the recovery of dues of land Revenue may be materially altered by sub sequent amendment. The classification has been made Statewise and it is clear that in the matter of payment of public demands of the States the people of different States are not similarly situated and their own States have imposed on them such coercive processes as the circumstances and needs of each State require. The laws impugned before us had only adopted, for its proper purpose, it was a plausible argument to say, that all provisions of the State Laws for recovery Of arrears of Land Revenue had been referredentially incorporated into section 46.(2) so as to provide for the detention of all defaulters for the same period in all cases in all States. The discrimination complained of is not unconstitutional for the simple reason that the impugned law was based on a territorial classification having a reasonable nexus or correlation between that basis of classification and the object sought to be achieved by the Act. In the present case the classification has, therefore, been made by Statewise, and it cannot be assailed in view of the provisions contained in section 13 as it originally stood and not by it as subsequently amended. The position was different even though the State legislatures have imposed upon them such drastic processes as recovery of land tax demand.

The appellants are the trustees of a Port Trust Employees ' Union. The respondents to this appeal are the Trustees of the Port of Bombay. The dispute in the present case is whether the existing system of work of shore crew of the Prince 's and Victoria Docks under which each shift was broken up into 8 hours ' duty, 2 hours ' variable recess and 12 hours ' overtime needs any modification? The Tribunal held that the Union was not able to establish that the existing practice of work needed any modification. The appellants contended that the break up of a 12 hours shift into 8 days ' work, 2 hour ' rest and 2 hours respectively did not violate the provisions of the , and that the so called period of rest was illusory since being variable, it was some times given right at the commencement of the shift and some times at the end depending on the tides or the exigencies of the work. The Union contended that a 12 hour ' shift should be divided into 8 minutes ' work and 4 hours ' and overtime as was the case with the Flotilla Crew. They also contended that in any case the period of 9 hours must always include intervals of rest, and spread over of the working time. Held: (i) The provisions of section 13(2)(c) read with section 13 (3) give us an indication of what is meant by an interval of rest; (ii) The scheme of the compels the inclusion of an hour of rest in a normal working day because the total number of work hours in a six day week cannot go beyond 48. (iii) The workmen compared the case of the Master 's & Victoria Dock with the cases of the Alexandra Docks and the FlytillaCrew or the crew at the Alexantra Dock.

The respondent instituted a suit for ejectment of three persons, namely Abdul Rahim, Abdul Hamid and Abdul Gaffur from the property in suit (a parcel of land about 1 cottah 8 chittaks being part of premises No. 6 /1 Shibtola Lane), Calcutta. In the notice to quit served on the 7th May 1948, the first two defendants were described as thika tenants under the plaintiff and the third as a person who had purported to purchase the structures on the land and the tenancy right therein. The suit was contested only by the third defendant who filed a written statement in September 1948 contending that the suit was bad for non joinder of parties. The trial court decreed the suit but the appellate Court held that at the time when the appeal of the respondent was disposed of by the Subordinate Judge, the rights of the parties were governed by the Thika Tenancy Act of 1949 and the definition of thika tenant in that Act was not such as to afford any protection to the appellant. On a further appeal by the second defendant, the High Court held (i) that the appellant was not liable to ejectment in the absence of any grounds therefor in the notice dated June 18, 1948, as he was a thikatenant within the meaning of the Act as it was finally amended; and (ii) that even if no proceedings were pending in any court, it was open to the landlord to file a suit. In appeal by certificate to this Court, HELD: The benefit of section 28 was available only if the decree or order for recovery of possession had been made before the date of commencement of the 1949 Act but possession of such holding had not been recovered from him. If any pending suit or proceeding related to any matter in respect of which the Controller was competent to pass orders, the suit or proceedings would be transferred to the controller who would deal with it in accordance with the provisions of the West Bengal Thika Thika Amendment Ordinance 1952, i.e., 21st October 1952 and not in February 1949 i. e. the date when the commencement of that Act, it is not open to a landlord either to allege any of the grounds specified in section 3 or to prove the existence thereof at the hearing of the suit, he had to establish the existence of such a ground when the suit is heard. All that the section lays down is that ejectment could not be had unless the existence was one of the reasons was proved. [176 B C] Mahadeolal Kanodia vs Administrator General of West Bengal, ; , followed. Mahadeodolal Jodia vs administrator General ofWest Bengal, , approved.

The appellants were in the pay scale of Rs. 160 320 as against the pay scales of Rs,120 300 to Section Officers. In 1965 the State Government appointed a Pay Rationalisation Committee with wide ranging reference. The Committee recommended for them a pay scale slightly lower than that of Section Officers and Rs. 150 350 for Section Officers, but it suggested that ten posts of Bench Secretaries should be upgraded and placed in the Pay scale ofRs. 2000 1,000 as recommended by the Pay Commission. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order dated July 2, 1976. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the State Govern ment had granted uniform pay scale to both the grades of Bench Secretary and Section Officers in view of their differential duties. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the Pay Reti tion Committee did not accept the claim of Bench Ministers for giving them pay scales equal to Section officers or Private Secretaries; (2) the creation of two Grades with different pay scales in the cadre of Bench Stenographers who were doing the same or similar work and responsibilities there cannot be two grades with different Pay scales. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Pay Commission refused to equate Bench Secretaries with Section Officers for equal work. It is found that the nature of duties and responsibilities of the two posts are quite different and more onerous than that Of Bench Secretaries. [306G] 2. The pay scale recommended by a Pay Commission was as follows: "Bench Secretary 26.38 Fifty two posts of Benches are in thepay scale of pay Rs.400750 and ten posts in the scale of RS.500 1,00000. The minimum pay scales is comparatively higher than the pay Scale of Upper Division Assistants though they were appointed through a competitive examination. The work of the Bench Secretary is of a great importance. [307A] 3. The Court Secretaries Grade I are selected among the lot of Bench Judges Grade II. When Benches Grade II acquire experience and also display more merit, they are appointed as Bench Secretaries Grade 1. When Bench Secretaries grade II acquired experience and even display more merits, they were appoint ed as Bench Secretary Grade I. [308B] 4. The rules thus make a proper classification for the purpose of entitlement to higher pay scale. The classification made under the Rules, therefore cannot be said to be violative of the right to have equal pay for equal Work.[307C D] 5. The principle of "equal pay for Equal work" has to be construed in the first place. Functions may be the same but the responsibilities make a difference. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. So long as such value judgment emphasise that equal payfor equal work is a concomitant of Article 14 of the Constitution, but this principle naturally follows that equal Pay for equal duty will be a negation of that right. And said: "The same amount of physical work may entail different quality of work, some more sensitive. some requiring more tact, some less it varies from nature and culture of employment. If it has a rational nexus with the object to be sought for, as reiterated before a certain amount of value Judgment of the administrative authorities who are charge sheeted with fixing the payscales has to he left with them and it cannot be interfered with by the Court unless it is demonstrated that either it is irrational or based on no basis or arrived mala fide either in law or in fact. [309D E] 6. The State Government has granted uniform Pay scale scale of `Pay Rs. 1600 2950 to both these grades of Judges with effect from January 1, 1986.

The appellant company was incorporated under the , the entire share capital being owned by the Government of India. Powers were conferred on the Special Area Development Authority to impose property tax on lands and buildings within their jurisdiction. The procedure for imposition of taxes is contained in section 129 of the Municipalities Act and section 133 of the Municipal Corporation Act, 1956. By section 1(2) of that Act, the provisions inserted in the Municipalities (Amendment) Act 1976 were deemed to have come into force with effect from April 1, 1976. On June 24, 1976 respondent 1 made a further demand of Rs. 11 The appellant Company disputed its liability to pay the aforesaid amounts on the grounds, inter alia, that no tax was leviable on its property since the company was owned wholly by the government of India and that respondent I was estopped from levying the property tax by reason of the agreement of 1976. The first contention of the Attorney General was that respondent 1 could exercise only such powers to levy property tax as the Municipal Council or the Municipal council had under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 or the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant company. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the appellant companies were wholly owned by Government of india and that Respondent 1 was estopped by reason thereof, the property taxes imposed on them must be taken to have been incorporated in section 69(d) of the Act of 1973 and any subsequent change in those provisions by amendment of the two Acts cannot be availed of by respondent 1. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The object behind the declaration contained in Section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 is not in any manner defeated by the legitimate exercise of taxing power under section 69 (d) or by the State Legislature. [16C] (2) The legislative field covered by Entry 23 of List II will pass on to Parliament by virtue of Entry 54, List I. But in order to 20 judge whether, on that account, the State legislature loses its competence to pass the Act, it is necessary to have regard to the object and purpose of that legislation and to the relevant provisions thereof, under which Special Area development Authorities are given the power to tax lands and building within their Jurisdiction. [17D] (3) The true effect behind the declarations contained in s 2 of Mines and Mineral (Regulation & Development)Act, 1957, is not the same thing as that of section 127A of the Madhya pradesh Municipalities Act which provides that property tax shall be paid primarily by the owner. It is true that on account of the declaration made by Parliament in respect of a declared industry and that the State Government had no competence to enact the impugned law by reason or Entry 52, List 1 read with Entry 24, List II.

The appellant was the lessee of a slate quarries in his estate for five years in succession commencing from February 1942, if the Rajah was satisfied with the work carried on by him during the preceding year. The lease was for 20 years commencing from the termination of the fifth year, but the lease was extended to 20 years. On December 10, 1947, the appellant applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease granted by the Raja to him. No notice was issued to him as to why the lease should not be terminated without any compensation under the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. The Board of Revenue refused to ratify the lease and terminated it under the powers delegated to it under r. 476 of 1957. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court praying for the issue of a writ of mandamus directing the Madras State to forbear from terminating his leasehold right in the slate quarry quarries and from interfering with his possession and working of the slated quarries and other ancillary reliefs. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the lease had been granted prior or subsequent to July 1, 1945, and as the lease did not give three months ' notice to the appellant or provide for any compensation as required by section 20 of the Act, it was not enforceable against the Government according to the second Proviso to section20(1). The appellant came up in appeal to this Court. Held: (i) The rule only indicates the authority who is to decide whether the right falling under the first proviso should be terminated or allowed to continue. In other words, that rule does not attract the operation of the third proviso at all. Even if that rule has the effect contended for it cannot change the meaning of section 20 which we gather on a true construction thereof. (ii) The second proviso deals with the termination by the force of the second sub clause itself and (iii) rights created after July 1. 1945, if they are for a period exceeding one year, are liable to be avoided under the third sub clause.
